1:
Origen fastens on the exact wording of the transition, that it is not all the sayings barely but all these sayings that are finished, and hears in the phrasing a deliberate movement toward the cross rather than a mere narrative seam. Hilary reads the sequence typologically: the Lord, having just foretold his return in splendour, announces his suffering immediately after, so that the disciples might learn the close connection between the sacrament of the Cross and the glory of eternity. Augustine takes up the harmonistic question the placing raises, reconciling the chronology here with John’s note of six days before the Passover at Bethany (John 12:1).

Jerome and Remigius dwell on the name of the feast. The Hebrew Phase, they insist, does not derive from the Greek word for suffering, as the similarity of sound tempts readers to suppose, but from passing over — the destroyer passing over the doors marked with blood (Exodus 12:13). Both then turn the etymology forward, finding in it Christ’s own passing out of this world to his Father, so that the night of the deliverance from Egypt and the night of his betrayal carry the same name for the same reason.

Calvin draws the doctrinal weight out of the prediction itself. This last forewarning clearly shows how willingly he offered himself to die, since God could not be appeased but by a sacrifice of obedience; and the announcement is made for the disciples’ sake, lest afterwards they be discouraged by supposing him dragged to death by necessity. Henry notices the contrast of preparations running in parallel: while his enemies were preparing trouble for him, he was preparing himself and his followers for it. He adds the pastoral observation that answers the obvious objection, since the disciples had already been told this more than once — after many distant notices we still have need of fresh ones.

Cyril of Jerusalem and Leo strike the note the others arrive at from their different directions. Cyril argues from foreknowledge: men who do not know what is coming die unwillingly, whereas Christ spoke beforehand of his passion and steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem, and did so lest the whole world should perish in its sins. Leo confesses that the festival partakes of so sublime a mystery as to surpass even the powers of great intellects, and yet holds that this is no reason for silence, the Church being one on which she may not hold her peace.
2:
Barnes and Clarke explain what the feast commemorated. The destroying angel passed over the houses of Israel marked with blood while the firstborn of Egypt fell (Exodus 12:13), and the one day of the Passover proper ran on into the seven days of unleavened bread, so that the name covered both a date and a season. Robertson sets the saying in the week by its tenses, marking cometh and is delivered up as futuristic presents and placing the words on the Tuesday evening, which is the beginning of the Jewish Wednesday, with the paschal meal falling on the Thursday evening. He notes that the same futuristic present recurs through the narrative, marking events already set in motion before they are enacted. Gill reaches the same day independently and explains why the disciples needed no further specification: the feast always began on a certain day, the fourteenth of the month Nisan, and the date was well known to them.

Ellicott enters the caution that keeps the reckoning honest. On the Jewish mode of counting, the point of time indicated here may be read either way, which is why the verse cannot by itself settle the disputed date of the supper (see John 13:1). The chronology is therefore firm about the interval and loose about the anchor.

Wesley pauses over the manner of the feast rather than its date, on the ground that it gives much light to several circumstances that follow. He describes the cup of wine solemnly blessed and divided (Luke 22:17), the supper begun with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, and the youngest person present asking the reason of the solemnity (Exodus 12:26). The detail matters because the Gospel narratives of the supper assume a ritual their first readers knew and later readers do not.

Cyril of Jerusalem reads the announcement as proof of a death freely chosen, since those who do not foreknow their end die unwillingly, where Christ spoke before of his passion. Leo sets beside it the scale of what is being announced, confessing that the Easter festival partakes of so sublime a mystery as to surpass even the powers of great intellects. The verse thus joins a precise interval of two days to the deeper fact that the one naming it was not being overtaken by events.
3:
The Gloss observes what the Evangelist is doing at this point in the narrative, laying bare the hidden springs and machinery by which the Lord’s Passion was brought to pass. Remigius draws the moral weight from the rank of the plotters, since the higher the station of those who band together for any villainy, the greater the enormity. Origen sharpens that into a charge: these were priests not of the people of God but of Gomorrah, conspiring against the firstborn of the whole creation (Colossians 1:15). Chrysostom finds the decay of the institution written into the very wording, since the Law allowed but one high priest for life, and the appearance of chief priests in the plural signals that the dissolution of the Jewish state was having its beginning.

Leo reads providence in their caution rather than piety. Their resolve to avoid the feast day arose not from reverence for the festival but from care for the success of their plot; and his point is that the care availed them nothing, since they could not succeed until the days of God’s appointing.

Barnes and Robertson supply the setting, identifying the assembly as the Sanhedrin and the place as the open court, the aulē, of the palace. Clarke and Robertson date the men: Caiaphas held the high priesthood from A.D. 18 to 36, with Annas his father-in-law beside him. Ellicott traces the plan to its origin, which lies further back than this meeting, since John 11:49–50 shows it formed after the raising of Lazarus, with the triumphal entry and the cleansing of the temple hastening what had already been decided. Lightfoot adds the rabbinic memory of dark portents reported forty years before the Temple was destroyed.

Calvin presses the chronology into an argument. The priests had resolved to delay for a time, which means that Christ’s fixing of the day was something no man could have suspected, and so proves he spoke by the spirit of prophecy rather than by inference from their mood. On their decision not to act during the feast, Calvin and Wesley draw the same lesson about whose timetable prevailed: contrary to their wish, God hastens the hour. When Judas came they changed their purpose, and so the counsel of God took place, and the true paschal Lamb was offered up on the great day after all.
4:
Barnes explains the constraint the council was working under. They did not dare to take him away openly lest the people should rise and rescue him, Jesus being regarded by the multitude as a distinguished prophet if not the Messiah; and they knew he lodged by night at Bethany, outside the city, which shaped the search for a place to seize him unobserved. Robertson reads their state of mind out of the grammar, taking the aorist middle for a deliberation that marks their puzzled condition: finding Jesus was never the difficulty, since his whereabouts were public and notice had already gone out for information (John 11:57). The difficulty was how to take him by subtilty, because the Triumphal Entry and the Tuesday debate in the temple had revealed the powerful following he had among the Galilean crowds.

Gill sets the meeting in the context of their earlier failures. The Jews had attempted his life more than once and in vain, which is why they now meet and consult together to form some scheme, and to do it in the most private manner they could manage.

Clarke turns to the outcome rather than the intention, and the contrast is his whole point. The providence of God frustrated their artful machinations, so that the event they wished to conduct with the greatest privacy and silence was transacted with all possible celebrity, amid the thousands who had resorted to Jerusalem for the feast. He then supplies the reason why this mattered and was not merely ironic: it was of the very first importance that the crucifixion of Christ be done openly and before a great concourse, so that the witnesses of the most essential act of redemption might be many rather than few.

Ellicott identifies what upset their timetable. The plan implied here, and in their resolve to avoid the feast, was hastened in its accomplishment by the unexpected treachery of Judas; they had meant to wait until the feast was over, but the temptation offered them proved too great to be resisted, and they became content to risk the very uproar among the people they had just decided to avoid. The rulers’ cunning was therefore real and effective on its own terms, and it served a counsel other than their own.
5:
Barnes explains the fear by the arithmetic of the festival. The feast drew a vast multitude from every part of Judea, Jerusalem swelling at such times, by the reckonings he cites, to something near three millions of people; and amid crowds on that scale there were frequent tumults and seditions, so that the Sanhedrin was justly apprehensive of what an open arrest of a popular teacher might set off. Robertson states the conclusion they drew, that the matter must be postponed until after the feast when the crowds had scattered, and that they might then take him by craft as one traps a wild beast. Clarke adds a sharper guess at whom they feared most, namely the Galileans, Jesus’ own countrymen, who were in the city in numbers for the feast.

Gill treats the decision as a formal one, reached upon mature deliberation and carried, if not unanimously, then at least by a majority, that nothing of this kind should be attempted on any of the days of the feast now at hand. He then notices that the resolve convicted them out of their own law, since their rules for dealing with a presumptuous offender required exactly the public execution at a feast that they were here determined to avoid. What they called prudence was a departure from their own procedure. Clarke turns that into a judgment on the men rather than the rule: whoever observes a festival on motives purely human violates it in his heart, and is a hypocrite before God.

Calvin reads the whole calculation as a case of restrained malice. Though those hungry dogs eagerly opened their mouths to devour Christ, God withheld them by a secret restraint from doing anything by their own deliberation or at their pleasure. They resolve on delay, and the delay does not hold. Calvin insists on why this is worth noticing rather than merely observing it: it is of great importance that we should know Christ was not overtaken by the plotting of men but offered at the hour appointed for him.

Wesley puts the reversal in the plainest form, and in doing so names what the verse records. This was the result of human wisdom; but when Judas came they changed their purpose, so that the counsel of God took place and the true paschal Lamb was offered up on the great day of the paschal solemnity. The men set the day by craft and found the day set for them.
6:
The largest question the older interpreters put to this scene is whether the four Gospels describe one woman or several. Origen and Chrysostom judge that Matthew, Mark and Luke are describing a single anointing, or else that Luke’s sinner is a different woman again, while John’s Mary of Bethany is another person altogether, the sister of Lazarus. Augustine distinguishes Luke’s Simon from this one. Jerome insists the woman who anointed the head and the woman who washed the feet with tears were not the same. Ambrose alone keeps the possibility of identity open, allowing that it may have been the same woman at two different times and two different stages of desert.

Chrysostom finds the host’s epithet doing work in the narrative rather than merely identifying him. The Evangelist names Simon’s leprosy to show what gave this woman her confidence: seeing that Jesus had cleansed the leper in whose house she stood, she trusted that he could cleanse the uncleanness of her soul. Hilary reads her figuratively, as the people of the Gentiles, who give glory to God in the passion of Christ.

Barnes and Robertson settle the identity from John, where she is Mary the sister of Lazarus (John 12:3), and describe the alabaster flask and the costly ointment that Mark calls spikenard. Lightfoot argues the other way and argues it strenuously: because the head is anointed here and the feet in John, this supper at Bethany cannot be the same occasion, and he places it before the Passover. Ellicott notices what the first two Evangelists do not say, calling their reticence in leaving her unnamed singular. Robertson adds that the feast was given by Simon, whom Jesus had healed of his leprosy, in honour of Jesus, and remarks drily that all sorts of fantastic theories have arisen over the woman’s identity.

Calvin is concerned with why the episode stands where it does. The anointing had happened a little before Christ came to Jerusalem, and is introduced here to show what suddenly drove the priests to make haste, since Judas’s indignation at it furnished them the opportunity they had not looked for. Henry reads the scene for its kindness rather than its chronology, hearing in it the singular kindness of a good woman to our Lord Jesus, offered in the house of a man whom Christ had likely cleansed of leprosy and did not disdain to converse with.
7:
Barnes and Ellicott name the woman from John 12:3 as Mary the sister of Lazarus and Martha. Barnes then describes the vessel: alabaster is a species of marble, light and of a beautiful white colour, much used by the ancients for preserving costly ointment, and the ointment itself was rare and difficult to obtain. Robertson adds the shape and the manner of using it, the flask named from the Egyptian town of alabaster, cylindrical and closed like a rosebud, with a slender neck broken off so that the whole of the precious contents might be poured out at once rather than measured.

Clarke surveys the dispute over whether this is the anointing of John 12 or another occasion, and Lightfoot presses what he takes to be decisive: it was not the same supper, for there our Saviour’s feet were anointed and here his head. Gill holds the question open from the other side, allowing that one and the same woman might perform a like action at different times, and distinguishing this from the anointing in the house of Simon the Pharisee.

Lightfoot then supplies the custom that makes the act legible. Oil perfumed with spices was very usual at feasts, especially sacred ones, and was wont to be poured on the head of someone present; he cites the school of Shammai on the order of the blessings, where the host holds sweet oil in his right hand and a cup of wine in his left. The anointing was therefore no eccentric gesture but a recognised mark of honour, and what distinguishes Mary is not the act but the measure.

Ellicott offers a conjecture to account for the silence of the first two Evangelists, suggesting she may have come in veiled, so that John alone knew who she was; otherwise it is hardly conceivable that they, or those from whom they had their knowledge, could have been ignorant of her name. Either way the identification matters less than the accounting. A known courtesy, ordinarily performed with a little oil on a guest of honour, is here performed with a flask whose neck has been snapped so that nothing can be kept back. The vessel Barnes describes was made to preserve its contents; Mary’s use of it ensured there would be nothing left to preserve.
8:
Barnes narrows the blame carefully. John says it was Judas who voiced the complaint, and Barnes allows that probably some of the others felt indignation, while Judas alone gave vent to his feelings, since he had the bag and was a thief (John 12:6). Ellicott traces the same narrowing across the records and finds it pointed: the limits contract from the disciples in Matthew to some in Mark to Judas alone in John (John 12:4), and he reads in the Traitor’s narrow, covetous soul one that could find in a lavish gift nothing but matter for reproach. Clarke and Lightfoot add the Hebrew idiom by which a plural may stand for the one who spoke, as the thieves at Matthew 27:44 means one thief and the doubters at Matthew 28:17 means Thomas.

Robertson weighs the word for waste, which reckons the thing a dead loss, nothing but sentimental aroma for the money spent, and he notes what the remark must have cost its hearer, calling it a cruel shock to Mary of Bethany. He observes too that Matthew says only that it might have been sold for much where Mark names three hundred pence, the vaguer figure leaving the indignation to speak for itself.

Calvin explains how a complaint from one mouth became a murmur in several. None of the others would ever have dared to complain if the wicked slander of Judas had not served as a torch to kindle them; once he had condemned the expense under a plausible pretext, the rest took up the grievance as their own. Gill states more simply what they saw, namely what a costly box of ointment it was and with what profusion she used it.

Wesley accepts both halves of the account without straining them, that several of them were angry and spoke, though none so warmly as Judas Iscariot. What the verse sets side by side, then, is Mary’s extravagance of love and the Traitor’s extravagance of greed, with the uncomfortable detail that a specious complaint passed easily from one false heart into several honest but mistaken ones.
9:
Barnes, Ellicott and Gill reckon the sum from the parallels, where Mark and John fix the value at three hundred pence. Ellicott translates that into labour, noting it comes near a whole year’s wages for a working man (Matthew 20:2) and would have fed a multitude (John 6:7). Gill works it out in two currencies, reckoning the Roman penny at sevenpence halfpenny, which brings three hundred of them to nine pounds seven shillings and sixpence, and the penny of the sanctuary at one and threepence, which doubles the sum; either way the ointment could well be called very precious and costly. The figure is not disputed by any of them; what they dispute is the use made of it.

Ellicott names what he calls the damning fact about the plea. The pretended zeal for the poor was the cloak for the irritation of disappointed greed, since the man who raised it was a thief and bore the bag (John 12:6). Lightfoot connects the cavil forward to the upper room, where the disciples heard Christ tell Judas to do quickly what he did and supposed he was being sent to give something to the poor (John 13:29) — a misunderstanding only possible because the pretext had been used before and had passed as plausible.

Barnes defends Mary on a different ground, and it is a question of right rather than of motive. The murmuring was without cause, because the ointment was her own property; she had a right to dispose of it as she pleased, answerable not to the disciples but to God. They had no authority over it and no cause of complaint even had she given the whole to Christ, which is what she did. Barnes adds that the murmur reached past Mary, since in grudging what was done there was an implied complaint against the Saviour for suffering it to be done at all.

Clarke draws the moral that closes the matter and widens it past Judas. How often does charity serve as a cloak for covetousness, God being sometimes robbed of his right under the pretence of devoting what is withheld to some charitable purpose to which there was never any intention of giving it. The appeal to the poor was specious, the gift to Christ was just, and the heart that grudged it was a thief’s before the ointment was ever poured.
10:
Robertson draws out the idiom in the question, which asks why they are giving the woman trouble, and reads it as an intervention: Jesus champions Mary’s act against a roomful of critics. He then generalises the difficulty the scene exposes, that it is hard for some people to allow others liberty for their own personalities to express themselves, and easy to raise small objections to devotion that does not take the form we would have chosen. Clarke renders the phrase as asking why they put the woman to pain, and explains the pain, since a generous mind is always wounded when its proffered kindness is refused.

Ellicott sharpens both halves of the sentence. Mark’s word shows the disciples were bitterly reproaching her, one after another, so that what Christ interrupts is not a passing remark but a chorus. And the work he commends is not merely good in the sense of useful: the word carries noble or honourable, which is precisely what the critics denied it, preferring the alms they had in mind to a deed of love done upon Christ himself. Barnes adds the two grounds on which it earned the name, that it was done with a mind grateful and full of love, and that it was besides preparative to his death (v.12).

Calvin faces the objection a careful reader will raise, that Christ, whose whole life was a rule of temperance and frugality, here appears to approve immoderate expense. His answer turns on the difference between a precedent and a case. Christ does not maintain that the woman did right in such a manner as to wish the same thing done every day; he maintains that what she had done in a single instance was agreeable to God, and agreeable for a particular reason, the honour of his approaching burial.

Gill observes how Christ came to know what to answer, distinguishing the two kinds of knowledge at work. As man he could read their minds partly by their looks and partly by their words; as God he knew the secret indignation and private resentment of their minds, which had not yet reached speech. On either account he rose at once to her defence, and the deed the disciples had called waste he named a good and honourable work — not as a rule for daily imitation, but as an act of love rightly timed.
11:
Barnes guards both duties at once. Regard for the poor is a plain precept of religion (Psalm 41:1; Proverbs 14:21; Galatians 2:10), and Christ would not prohibit it; but every duty should be done in its place, and the duty then incumbent was Mary’s. He adds from Mark the clause that makes the asymmetry plain, that whensoever they will they may do the poor good, since the poor would never cease out of the land (Deuteronomy 15:11), where the hour for honouring Christ’s body would not return. Clarke puts the same contrast in Christ’s own voice: his bodily presence was about to be removed from them for ever, and the woman, under a presentiment of his death, was preparing him for burial.

Ellicott notices the tactics of the reply, that the Lord met the objection on its own ground rather than exposing the man who raised it. There is no open rebuke of the dishonest objector; but by look and tone, in saying that they would not always have him, the Traitor was made to feel he stood before one who read the secrets of his heart. The answer was therefore public in its terms and private in its aim.

Calvin uses the verse for a polemical caution, and it is the limit of the precedent that concerns him. Christ does not simply defend the anointing so that we may imitate it, but assures us that it pleased God on some particular account; and this must be carefully weighed, lest we fall into the error of contriving expensive modes of worshipping God, as he says the Papists do, who draw from this text a defence of incense, wax tapers, splendid decorations and pompous exhibitions.

Wesley reads the permanence of the poor as a mercy rather than a melancholy fact. Such is the wise and gracious providence of God that we may always have opportunities of relieving them, and so of laying up for ourselves treasures in heaven. The balance the verse keeps is therefore not between a greater duty and a lesser but between a perpetual one and an unrepeatable one, and the unrepeatable had claim on that evening.
12:
Robertson credits Mary with an understanding the apostles lacked. She alone had understood what Jesus had repeatedly said about his approaching death, while the disciples, wrapped up in their own notions of a political kingdom, failed to sympathise with him as he faced the cross. With a woman’s fine intuitions she did begin to understand, and the anointing was her way of expressing her high emotions and loyalty. He notes that the verb used is the one for preparing a body for burial (John 19:40).

Lightfoot states the claim more boldly than Robertson will. She, and she first, believes that Christ should die, and under that conviction pours the ointment on his head as though anointing it for burial. Clarke supports the reading from the Septuagint’s use of the word for embalming (Genesis 50:2), and observes that Christ took this opportunity to tell the company plainly that he was shortly to die.

Ellicott hears the words landing on ears not ready for them. They must have fallen with a strange sadness on men who expected the kingdom immediately to appear, and the enthusiasm of the moment made them deaf to the real import of what they heard; their Master alone of all that company knew that the fragrance of that perfume would not have died away before his body was laid in the sepulchre. Barnes guards the claim from being overstated: it is not to be supposed Mary clearly understood that he was then about to die, since the apostles did not fully comprehend it, but she had acted in kindness and love, and Christ pronounced the act a proper preparation for burial, bodies being anciently anointed and embalmed for the sepulchre.

Calvin adds the figure he finds underneath the act, and it turns the ointment into a sign rather than a courtesy. Christ valued it not on account of its odour but solely in reference to his burial, as a symbol that his grave would yield a sweet odour, breathing life and salvation through the whole world (John 12:7). Wesley is more cautious about Mary’s intention, granting that this was not her design, and that our Lord puts this construction upon it in order to confirm what he had already said of his approaching death. On either reading the gift became the embalming of a body soon to be given for the life of the world, whether or not the giver had grasped as much when she broke the flask.
13:
Clarke treats the saying as evidence, calling it another remarkable proof of the prescience of Christ. A matter which, humanly speaking, depended on mere fortuitous circumstances has stood as firm and regular as the ordinances of heaven; and he draws a figure out of the act itself, that as embalming preserves a body from decay, so her deed should be preserved by the gospel’s telling of it.

Ellicott concedes the obvious objection before answering it. The prediction tended in some measure to bring about its own fulfilment, since a saying recorded is thereby remembered. What cannot be explained that way is the prevision of a universal extension of the gospel, uttered at such a moment, which he ranks among the proofs of a foreknowledge not less than divine. His contrast makes the point: others at that table saw victory only, and that immediate, where he saw condemnation and shame and death, and through them a victory. Barnes states the plainer ground on which the deed is recorded, as a memorial of her piety and self-denial, adding that the good deeds of the pious should be recorded and had in recollection.

Calvin reads the promise as a verdict reversing a verdict. The act will do honour to Mary because it will be praised by the doctrine of the gospel, from which he draws the rule that we ought to estimate our works not by the opinion of men but by the testimony of the word of God. He also notices what the promise does to the men who had just spoken: in foretelling that all nations with one consent will applaud this action, Christ indirectly censures his disciples, whose own company had grudged it an hour before.

Cyril of Jerusalem fastens on the gospel that was to be preached rather than on the woman, and turns to the eternal life it offers, that whoever believes on the Son has everlasting life (John 6:47). That is the message in whose telling her memory was to travel, which is what the promise actually says: not that she would be famous, but that she would be carried wherever the gospel went.
14:
Chrysostom fastens on the connecting word and makes it a clue to motive. Then, he says, meaning when Judas heard that the gospel should be preached everywhere, for that made him afraid. Raban insists on the freedom of the act against any excuse that might be offered for it: he was neither compelled nor invited, but of his own free will formed the wicked design. Leo supplies the anatomy of the passion that drove it, that in comparison of the love of money all our other affections are feeble, and that there is no trace of righteousness left in a heart where covetousness has once taken up its abode.

Barnes brings in what Luke adds, that Satan entered into Judas (Luke 22:3), and explains the point of entry as his ruling passion of avarice, the temptation finding a door already open. Robertson sets the two figures of the chapter against each other, Mary and Judas as extreme opposites, she freely spending in love and he willing to sell his Master for money; and he presses the connection between them, that her act of love provoked Judas to his despicable deed.

Calvin marks the hardening rather than the greed. Christ’s admonition at the table was so far from producing any change in him that he went away immediately afterwards to transact an infamous bargain, the warning serving only to settle him in his purpose. Henry sets the two deeds side by side as the chapter does, the greatest unkindness following hard upon the greatest kindness, and finds the aggravation in the man’s standing, since the traitor was one of the twelve.

Jerome and Origen look for a fittingness in the figure agreed on. Jerome notes that the wretch does not demand any fixed sum, as a man selling something of value would, but leaves it to the buyers to determine what they will give, in the manner of one disposing of a worthless slave; and he sets the transaction beside Joseph sold by his brethren. Origen observes a correspondence in the number itself, thirty pieces of silver answering to the thirty years the Saviour had dwelt in the world before his ministry began, and both find it dark that any price at all was named for the one who had come to redeem the whole world.
15:
Lightfoot fixes the sum from the law and the rabbis. Citing Maimonides, he gives the price of a slave as thirty selaim of pure silver (Exodus 21:32), payable whether the slave be worth a hundred pounds or a single penny, and he adds the weight, a selaa reckoned at three hundred and eighty-four barleycorns. The figure is therefore not a bribe arrived at by haggling but a fixed statutory valuation, which is what makes it an insult rather than an offer.

Clarke notes the reading that gives staters, a stater being the shekel and worth about three shillings, and cannot resist the comment it invites: a goodly price for the Saviour of the world. Wesley reckons the whole at about three pounds fifteen shillings sterling, and names it likewise the price of a slave. Ellicott reads the priests’ side of the bargain as contempt rather than thrift, since the reward was relatively a small one, and the chief priests, seeing through the sordid baseness of the man in front of them, gauged what he was worth and paid accordingly (compare Zechariah 11:12).

Barnes notices the terms of payment and what they imply about the trust between the parties. They promised the money without handing it over, lest the man deceive them, so that the silver was paid only after the deed was done (Matthew 27:3; Acts 1:18). He observes too that Mark and Luke record only a promise of money, which in the original is silver, where Matthew alone preserves the exact and ominous figure.

Robertson hears the cold initiative in the seller’s own words. Judas asks what they are willing to give him, and the colloquial turn of the clause that follows, with its emphatic I will deliver him, shows the aspect of the transaction: the proposal comes from him, not from them. Gill identifies the men addressed as the chief priests, to whom Judas had come with his offer. What the whole exchange settles, then, is that the sum was a slave’s purchase, weighed out as Zechariah had foretold, and that it measures the Traitor’s baseness and the priests’ scorn in the same figure.
16:
Robertson reads the diligence of the crime out of the tense. The imperfect shows a continued search for a good chance, and his comment is bleak: Judas went at his business and stuck to it. Barnes and Gill add Luke’s qualification, that the opportunity wanted was one in the absence of the multitude (Luke 22:6). That identifies the difficulty precisely. Finding Jesus was never hard; delivering him to the priests without the people knowing, and without exciting a tumult, was the whole problem, and it was the one point on which Judas and the priests were already agreed. Barnes also defines the act being sought, since the word for betraying means to deliver a man into the hands of an enemy by treachery, which is what distinguishes it from a simple arrest.

Gill fills in what the traitor was waiting for and why. Prompted on by Satan and by the lucre of the money, he looked for the most private occasion, when Christ was alone, so that no tumult might arise and there might be no danger of a rescue. The patience is part of the offence: a man hunting a safe hour is not a man swept away.

Clarke works from the word for opportunity, which means a convenient or fitting season, and turns the verse into an observation about how sin finishes what it starts. Men seldom leave a crime imperfect; once sin is conceived it meets in general with few obstacles until it brings forth death. The betrayal was therefore no sudden passion but a fixed design pursued with method.

Clarke then breaks out against the motive in borrowed words, reaching for Virgil’s cry over a murder committed for gold — to what dost thou not drive the hearts of men, O cursed hunger for gold? The citation is deliberate on his part, since a heathen poet had seen the same thing without the help of revelation, and the love of money needs no particular faith to be recognised as deceitful and deeply damning. What the verse records, on every account given of it, is a sin already settled in the heart and now simply hunting its hour.
17:
Clarke explains how the day could be called the first at all. Strictly the feast of unleavened bread began on the fifteenth (Leviticus 23:5–6), but since the Jews began eating unleavened bread on the fourteenth (Exodus 12:18), that day was often termed the first. Jerome fixes the same date and adds the marks by which it was known: the fourteenth, when the lamb is killed, the moon is at full, and leaven is put away, the New Testament here keeping the practice of the Old. Chrysostom accounts for the usage differently, by the Jewish reckoning of a day from the evening, so that the first day means the day on whose evening the passover was killed.

Robertson names the famous controversy the verse opens, on the apparent disagreement between the Synoptics and the Fourth Gospel (John 18:28). Ellicott states both sides without resolving them: the precision of the first three Gospels leaves no room for doubt that they looked on the Last Supper as the celebration of the actual Paschal Feast, while John leaves a different impression. Calvin takes the day to refer to the following one, the killing being at hand, and Henry draws the doctrinal point from whichever reckoning is adopted, that Christ, being made under the law, submitted to all its ordinances, and died the day after the passover.

Remigius asks the question the typology invites: if the lamb figured Christ, why did he not suffer on the night it was killed? His answer is that on this night he committed to his disciples the mysteries of the new covenant, so that the figure gave way to the thing figured at the table before it did so at the cross. Origen presses the consequence against the Ebionites, that we do not keep the Passover with Jewish observances but celebrate spiritually what they performed in figure (Galatians 4:4).

Hilary and Raban find significance in an omission, that the householder’s name is withheld, so that all who would receive Christ within the dwelling place of their own minds may know the opportunity is theirs. Augustine explains the odd phrasing on grammatical grounds instead, that Matthew’s such a man is said for brevity’s sake, since no man speaks so in actual address, and conveys only that the disciples were sent to one particular person.
18:
Robertson explains the curious phrase, which he identifies as the only instance in the New Testament of an old Attic idiom, the equivalent of our Mr X. Jesus may well have named the man, and Mark and Luke supply instead the sign the disciples were to follow, a man bearing a pitcher of water (Mark 14:13; Luke 22:10). Gill suggests who that figure would have been, seemingly a servant sent out on an errand, since carrying water was not the householder’s own work. Gill also fixes where the disciples were standing when they received the order, still at Bethany or on the Mount of Olives, outside the city, so that the errand began with a walk into Jerusalem.

Ellicott and Barnes judge the master of the house to have been probably a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews, one of the many such believers in Jerusalem, which would explain both his readiness and the discretion with which the arrangement was made. Barnes adds from Luke that the two sent were Peter and John. Clarke, citing Grotius, explains the idiom as the form the Greeks used of a particular person so well known that there was no need to specify him by name, which suits a man with whom Christ was well acquainted and whom the disciples knew. Robertson ventures a guess at the house, that it may have been the home of Mary the mother of John Mark.

Calvin reconciles the accounts rather than choosing between them. Matthew specifies a certain man where the others report a sign given as though to an unknown individual; but it cannot be doubted that when the disciples came to the house they found it was one of their acquaintances. He then notices the tone of the message itself, that Christ enjoins the man authoritatively to make ready a lodging — a small but real mark of lordship in one who is on his way to die.

On the phrase about his time, Clarke and Robertson agree it means the time of his crucifixion, and Clarke shows from Kypke that the word denotes the appointed season rather than a span of hours. Wesley reads it the same way, that the Master’s time at hand is the time of his suffering. The errand therefore holds two things together: the homely business of borrowing an upper room, and the settled consciousness of a man arranging the place of his last Passover while knowing exactly what the hour is for.
19:
Barnes itemises what the preparation involved, and the list is longer than a modern reader expects. They procured a paschal lamb, had it killed and flayed by the priests with the blood poured out at the altar, roasted it, and prepared the bitter herbs, the sauce and the unleavened bread. Ellicott adds the furnishing of the room itself, the couches, the lamb, bread, herbs, wine and conserve of sweet fruits. Clarke notes, with Wakefield, that the Jews considered the passover a sacrificial rite, Josephus himself calling it a sacrifice, so that the errand was in its own way a priestly one. Ellicott adds how the room itself would have been set out, the tables arranged probably in the form of a Roman triclinium and the benches covered with cushions.

Gill narrates the errand as it unfolded: they went into the city, met the man carrying his pitcher of water home, followed him into the house he entered, addressed the master of it in the manner Christ had directed, and were shown a large upper room already furnished with everything proper for the occasion, exactly as they had been told they would be. Lightfoot names the two sent as Peter and John (Luke 22:8) and lays out the steps they had to take, the lamb being bought, approved and then slain. He also makes an observation about the other man at that table which the verse does not state but the chronology requires: the two who went only knew that Judas was about some other business, while the rest supposed he was preparing necessaries.

Calvin reads the compliance as a pattern of faith, and begins from the doubt the errand could reasonably have raised. In seeking out an unknown man they might well have wondered whether they would obtain what they asked, aware as they were that their Master was everywhere hated. Yet they make no anxious inquiry about the result, but peaceably obey; and Calvin turns that into the standing requirement, that if we are desirous to have our faith approved we must learn the like ready submission.

What the verse records is therefore a short sentence covering a long afternoon’s work. The disciples ask where, are told, and simply do it, leaving the outcome with the one who sent them — while one of their own number is away on an errand of his own, and the preparation of the Passover goes forward with nobody at the table yet knowing what the meal will become.
20:
Barnes fixes the hour from the law, the lamb being killed between the evenings (Exodus 12:6) and the supper eaten after sunset, often well into the night (Exodus 12:8). Robertson corrects the posture a reader is likely to assume: the verb means he was reclining, lying on the left side with the right hand free, for although the first Passover in Egypt was eaten standing and in haste (Exodus 12:11), later custom had settled into reclining. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic distinction between sitting and lying, that is, leaning on the left side upon couches. Clarke raises the question whether Christ kept the Passover some hours before the Jews generally did, on the same day but not at the same hour.

Jerome reads the evening for what Christ does with it. Having already foretold his Passion, he now foretells the traitor, and does so in a way that gives him place of repentance, designating him and yet not by name. Chrysostom gives the same motive and adds a second: Christ declared the treachery out of regard for Judas, to bring him to a better mind, and also to assure the rest that he did not suffer through weakness. Leo states the principle underneath the restraint, that the wickedness was met not with a harsh and open rebuke, so that penitence might find a readier way back in one who had not been disgraced by public dismissal.

Remigius explains the phrase that names the company, since the traitor is counted in it. He sat with the twelve because Judas was personally among them, though he had ceased to be one of them in merit. Raban adds a homely detail of the table itself, that the dish into which the Lord and the traitor reached together may have been a square earthen vessel, and that the exchange between them was not overheard by the rest.

Calvin places the moment in the sequence of the rite, reading the supper as following the solemn close of the paschal ceremony, after which Christ came to table. So the scene is set with some care by all of them: the Lord reclining in the ordinary posture of a feast, the Twelve about him, the traitor counted among them, and the coming betrayal met not with exposure but with a mercy that leaves a door open.
21:
Barnes brings in from John what Matthew does not record of the manner, that Jesus was troubled in spirit and testified (John 13:21), bearing witness rather than merely remarking; and he reads the trouble as a response to the greatness of the crime Judas was about to commit. Robertson describes the effect on the room, calling the announcement a bolt from the blue for everyone except Judas, who was startled for a different reason, to learn that Jesus understood his treacherous bargain. Clarke glosses the verb as will deliver me up, noting that the betrayal in the sense of the bargain had already happened, and what remained was the handing over.

Gill sets the words in their occasion. The discourse fell while they were eating the lamb, the bread and the bitter herbs, at the point in the meal when it was usual to speak at length about the reason and design of the institution, so that the announcement broke into a holy conversation rather than a silence.

Calvin presses the aggravation, which is for him the whole force of the verse. To make the treachery of Judas more detestable, Christ points out its aggravated baseness, that the man was meditating the betrayal of his own intimate friend while seated at the holy banquet. Had a stranger done this, Calvin says, it would have been more easily endured; that one of his intimate friends should, after entering into an infamous bargain, be present at the sacred table was incredibly monstrous.

Ellicott attends to what the words leave unsaid, finding them intentionally vague as if to rouse the others to self-questioning. His reason is uncomfortable and precise: the eleven were guiltless of Judas’s crime, but they had yielded to tendencies — the murmuring over the ointment (v.8), the quarrelling about precedence that they were shortly to renew — which were dragging them down towards his level. The announcement is therefore pitched to wound the one and to examine the rest, plain enough to reach a conscience already sold and vague enough to summon every other conscience in the room.
22:
Barnes reads the reaction as evidence of character. John reports that they looked on one another, and each of them, Judas excepted, was conscious of no such intention and began to examine himself; that willingness to know themselves showed their innocence and their attachment to Jesus, and Barnes treats it as the mark of the true Christian spirit. He notes too how sensitive they proved to the least suspicion of the kind, the grief coming before any defence. Robertson supports the reading from the grammar, since the form of the question expects the answer no, which was natural for every man at the table except the one who had to bluff it out using the same form a few verses later.

Ellicott and Lightfoot fill in John’s fuller account of what else was happening (John 13:22): the perplexed glances round the table, Peter’s whisper to John, and the sign of the sop, all of it passing as a by-play unheard by the other disciples. Lightfoot notes that in that exchange the Lord had privately disclosed the person to John only, which is why the open question here belongs to a more public moment and leaves the rest still ignorant.

Gill breaks their sorrow into its causes, which were three rather than one: that Christ should be betrayed at all into the hands of enemies who would use him ill, that so vile an action should be done by one from among themselves, and chiefly that they could not conceive which of them could be guilty of such a sin. Clarke marks the one discordant note in the room. The eleven were truly sorrowful, while the hypocritical traitor endeavoured to put on the appearance of sorrow, matching their grief without sharing it. Clarke cannot account for the attempt and says so, wondering whether the love of money had so blinded the man as to leave him incapable of discerning what he had long known, that Christ read the secrets of the soul.

Calvin is careful to distinguish what the sorrow was. He does not think the disciples were alarmed as persons struck with terror; rather, abhorring the crime, they are desirous to clear themselves from the suspicion of it. He then names what he admires in their manner, calling it a mark of reverence that when indirectly blamed they do not reply angrily or turn on one another, but each man constitutes himself his own judge. The instinct the verse records is therefore neither indignation at the charge nor accusation of a neighbour, but sorrow and honest self-scrutiny in men whose chief fear was to be found unfaithful.
23:
Barnes and Clarke explain the dish and what was in it. The bitter sauce, the charoseth, was made of raisins, vinegar and other seasoning, its colour and consistency recalling the clay of the Egyptian bondage, and the bread was dipped into it. Clarke adds the detail that gives the saying its force: families used several little dishes set about different parts of the table, so that Judas’s dipping into the same one as the Lord marks him as reclining near at hand. Robertson describes the platter as holding the broth of nuts and raisins and figs into which the bread was dipped before eating, and notes that they all dipped their hands, having no knives, forks or spoons.

Robertson draws the conclusion the narrative requires, that the words identify one of those who had dipped and nothing more precise, and that it is plain Judas was not recognised by the rest. Ellicott offers the explanation that accounts for what follows, supposing the words were spoken to a few only, those nearest their Master; otherwise Judas could scarcely have ventured the question he puts two verses later.

Calvin holds that this was deliberate. Christ neither removes their doubt nor points out the person of Judas, but only confirms that the traitor is one of their own number. Being left in suspense and perplexity for a time was hard, and Calvin thinks it had its use, since it made them contemplate the atrocity of the crime rather than merely identify its author.

The second use Calvin finds is retrospective, and it is about Scripture rather than psychology. Afterwards they were able to see that the prediction of the psalm had been fulfilled in front of them, that the man who ate pleasant food with him had lifted up his heel against him (Psalm 41:9). On that reading the disclosure is veiled on purpose: the table-fellow who shares the dish is named as the betrayer, and named so generally that the eleven still cannot tell which of them is meant, while the Scripture of the trusted friend turned enemy quietly completes itself before their unseeing eyes.
24:
Barnes takes the verb for going as a Hebrew idiom for dying (Genesis 15:2), and locates the writing appealed to in the Old Testament, comparing Psalm 41:9 with John 13:18 and adding Isaiah 53:4–9 and Daniel 9:26; Luke renders the same clause as it was determined. Ellicott calls this the first direct reference of the coming passion to the Scriptures, and then states the balance the verse holds without softening either side: it was appointed that the Christ should suffer, but that appointment did not make men less free agents, nor diminish the guilt of what they did, which is how Peter speaks of it afterwards (Acts 1:16).

Robertson refuses the modern softening outright. There are some today who seek to palliate the crime of Judas, where Jesus here pronounces his terrible doom; and Robertson adds the detail that settles the matter for him, that Judas heard it and went on.

Calvin meets the offence of the thing directly. What could seem more unreasonable than that the Son of God should be betrayed by a disciple? His answer is that Christ declares all this to take place only by the will of God, and proves it by the testimony of Scripture; and the proof is not an excuse, since the decree under which the deed falls does nothing to acquit the man who commits it.

Wesley and Clarke fasten on the woe rather than the decree. Wesley extends it past the traitor, asking whether the same may not be said of every man who finally perishes, and uses the verse against the hope of a universal salvation. Lightfoot notes that the form of words was very usual among the Talmudists, who said of a wicked man that it were better for him that he had not been created, so that Christ is speaking a known idiom rather than coining a phrase. Clarke weighs the doom against any notion that it could be said of a man for whom a release remained after suffering, and reads the woe as final. Cyril of Jerusalem keeps the other half of the verse in view, that Christ shunned not death, lest the whole world should perish in its sins.
25:
Barnes glosses the two words of the reply: thou hast said means thou hast said the truth, it is so, thou art the man, the same idiom that recurs at the trial (compare Matthew 26:64 with Mark 14:62). Gill notices when the question came, that Judas put his only after all the rest had put theirs, so that the form was borrowed and the timing calculated. Gill adds that the man had already taken his step toward the deed and was seeking the opportunity to complete it, so that the question was put by one waiting on the servants of the chief priests.

Clarke marks the effrontery of it. The man knew in his own conscience that he had already struck the bargain, and still he asks whether it is he — asking, Clarke adds, in the hope that he had transacted his business so privately that it had not yet transpired. Clarke also catches a difference of address that the English flattens: each of the others had said Lord, where Judas dares not, and says only Rabbi.

Ellicott connects the moment to John’s account and reads it as something harder than concealment. After the sop Satan entered into him (John 13:27), and the question is reckless defiance rather than caution, a man asking whether his Master really knows. The reply, Ellicott notes, was not heard by all (John 13:29), only the command to do quickly what he did, which is why the rest of the table could still misunderstand what was happening.

Calvin probes the psychology of hardened guilt, and the paradox interests him. Though we often see persons trembling who are conscious of doing wrong, there is mingled with the fear such stupidity that they boldly make a flat denial. Judas, restrained by an evil conscience, cannot remain silent; he is tormented and overwhelmed with fear and anxiety by that internal executioner, and the question is forced out of him by the very thing he is trying to hide. What the exchange yields, then, is a hypocrite who has already sold his Lord still daring to ask, and a Lord who in two words lets him know that everything is known — which was itself a mercy, had the man taken it so.
26:
Jerome marks the transition the moment represents: the typical Passover being ended, Christ passes to the true paschal sacrament, offering what Melchizedek had foreshadowed in bread and wine (Genesis 14:18), the present verity of his Body and Blood. The Gloss explains why the gift comes under another kind than its own, that faith might have its merit. Augustine faces the awkward fact that the disciples did not receive fasting, and defends the Church’s later discipline nonetheless, that the Lord’s Body should enter the Christian’s mouth before other food. Cyril of Jerusalem presses the effect on the recipient, that the faithful are thereby made of the same body and blood with Christ.

Chrysostom, Leo and Hilary turn to the man still at the table. After the sop Satan entered into him (John 13:27), and what aggravates the sin for them is not the betrayal alone but that he came near to these mysteries with such a heart.

Wesley states the Reformed reading of the words without hedging: this bread is, that is, signifies or represents my body, according to the style of the sacred writers (Genesis 40:12; Galatians 4:24), and Barnes agrees that it represents his body. Robertson adds a textual correction that bears on the usual language about the rite: the genuine text of 1 Corinthians 11:24 omits the word broken, and his body was not broken (John 19:33), whatever is done to the bread. Calvin reads the two elements as a single lesson, that Christ employed two symbols to show that our life is shut up in him, supplying in himself the place of meat and drink.

Henry fixes the timing, that this happened as they were eating, at the latter end of the passover supper, the new ordinance coming in the room of the old because Christ our passover is sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7). The division that runs through all of this is over the mode and not the reverence: the older interpreters press a real participation in the Body, the Reformed a sign that seals the same union by faith, and neither side treats the bread as merely bread.
27:
Remigius reads the giving of the cup as an expression of gladness, since in handing them the cup of his Blood Christ shows what joy he has in our salvation; he recalls the blood of the covenant sprinkled by Moses (Exodus 24:8), and notices the exact wording of the promise, that it is said not for a few, nor for all, but for many. The Gloss explains why two elements are used at all, bread and wine being set apart for the representation of his Passion, in which his blood was separated from his Body. Cyprian and Ambrose press the mingling of water with the wine, answering to the water that flowed with the blood from his pierced side.

Chrysostom fastens on the thanksgiving rather than the cup. He gave thanks in order to instruct us, and showed thereby that he came not to his Passion against his will — a man does not give thanks for what is being forced upon him. Jerome takes the fruit of the vine that he will drink anew in the Father’s kingdom of the joy of a redeemed Israel, and Augustine reads the same promise of the immortality of renewed bodies, the new wine answering to the old body given up in the Passion. Hilary draws a sterner inference from it, that Judas had not drunk with him, being unworthy of the communion of eternal sacraments, while to all who did partake he promises that they shall drink with him hereafter.

Barnes and Ellicott set the cup in its place in the meal, identifying it with the cup of the Hallel and noting that it was taken after supper (1 Corinthians 11:25; compare v.30). Ellicott observes that later ritual passed a cup round three times, one of which has already appeared at Luke 22:17, so that the question is which cup rather than whether there were several. Clarke and Lightfoot work through the paschal cups and the blessings attached to each.

Calvin states the pastoral aim of the two symbols together, which is to keep our faith wholly fixed on Christ himself. As the body requires both meat and drink, so he supplies the place of both, which Calvin calls an astonishing display of his grace. Whatever the difference over the mode, the cup is given with thanksgiving and given to be shared by all, as the seal of blood poured out for many.
28:
Barnes reads the words as he read those over the bread, that this represents his blood, and notes that Luke and Paul give the saying in another form, that this cup is the new testament in his blood (1 Corinthians 11:25). He also fixes the referent precisely: by the cup Christ meant the wine in it and not the vessel, pointing to the one and saying of the other that it represented blood about to be shed. On the English word testament both Barnes and Clarke hold that covenant is the right rendering, and Clarke warns against the popular error that takes the New Testament for the printed book when what is meant is the new covenant itself.

Robertson explains the Greek term, which serves both for a covenant and for a will, and becomes operative at death (Hebrews 9:15–17). He adds the Hebrew background that makes the gesture legible, since to make a covenant was to cut up the sacrifice (Genesis 15:9), so that the cup is the seal of a covenant cut, like the ancient ones, in sacrificial blood. Ellicott and Robertson both note a textual point, that the best manuscripts omit the word new in this verse, probably introduced later to bring the text into harmony with Luke’s report.

Gill treats the cup as an emblem of the precious blood by which the new dispensation of the covenant of grace was ratified and confirmed, and lists what it conveys: peace, pardon, righteousness and eternal life. He points back to the blood sprinkled at the making of the first covenant (Exodus 24:8), which is the rite this one answers.

The word many is taken two ways. Wesley reads the scope wide, taking it of as many as spring from Adam. Cyril of Jerusalem reaches instead for the Psalm, finding in the table prepared before him (Psalm 23:5) the mystical table now set in the place of the table of devils. What none of them disputes is the thing the cup is said to be: blood of the covenant, poured out unto the remission of sins.
29:
Barnes takes the words first as a farewell. They mark the point at which the observance of the passover, and of the rites shadowing forth future things, comes to an end: he is about to die, and this is the last time he will partake of them with his disciples, until the Father’s kingdom is established and they share the blessings and triumphs the types foretold. On his reading the new drinking is the reality of which the paschal cup was the shadow. Gill draws an inference about the cup just passed, that Christ had himself drunk of it, since none might eat before the man who blessed and broke the bread had tasted it.

Clarke renders the promise as wine of a widely different nature, such as the kingdom of God shall produce. Ellicott prefers the rendering I shall not drink, hearing in it an acceptance of what God had ordained rather than a resolution of Christ’s own, and takes the new wine of the kingdom of God completed and perfected. Robertson cautions against pressing the phrase about the fruit of the vine, noting from the papyri that the language of the Messianic banquet does not make it obligatory to employ literal wine; he adds that the wording rather implies Jesus himself partook of the bread and the wine, though it is not distinctly stated. Clarke takes the first clause more modestly still, as intimating no more than that they would have no further opportunity of eating this bread and drinking this wine together, the crucifixion being a few hours off.

Calvin observes what the saying did for the men who heard it, warning them at once of their Master’s departure and of the hope lying beyond it. On the question of exactly where in the meal the words fell he declines to spend effort, judging it of little importance at what precise moment Christ said this.

Wesley puts the whole verse in the plainest terms, that he shall taste no more wine until he drinks wine of quite another kind in the glorious kingdom of his Father, and that of this the disciples shall also partake with him. The last clause is what keeps the verse from being merely an announcement of death. A parting cup is also a pledge: the fellowship broken that night is promised again at a table where the shadow has given way to the thing itself.
30:
Gill, Barnes, Clarke and Wesley all identify the hymn as the Hallel, Psalms 113–118, sung in two parts at the Passover by the universal consent of Jewish antiquity. Robertson corrects the impression that the company left immediately, since Jesus tarried for the discourse and prayer of John 14–17, perhaps moving out into the street after John 14:31; the old requirement to stay indoors until morning (Exodus 12:22) was no longer binding. Wesley adds that Olivet lay about two miles from Jerusalem. Hilary reads the singing itself as a sign, that men confirmed by the powers of the Divine mysteries are exalted to heavenly glory in a common joy and gladness.

Chrysostom turns the singing into a reproof of his own congregation, aimed at those who will not stay for the final prayer in the sacred mysteries, since that last prayer answers to this hymn. Raban notes that Peter understood the singing in the same spirit. His complaint is sharper still against those who rise from the table drunk when they should have given thanks and closed with a hymn; Christ gave thanks before and sang afterwards, that we should do the same.

Jerome and Origen read the ascent as well as the song. Jerome bids whoever is filled upon the bread and cup of Christ praise God and ascend the Mount of Olives, where there is refreshment after toil. Origen makes the movement itself the lesson, that they go from height to height, because the believer can do nothing in the valley. Raban connects the hymn with the thanksgiving of John 17 and with the Psalm where the poor eat and are filled and praise the Lord (Psalm 22:26).

Hilary and Jerome both look ahead to what is about to be said on that road. Hilary notes that Christ’s prediction of the scattering is supported by old prophecy, that God will smite the shepherd (Zechariah 13:7). Jerome marks the emphasis on this night, the particular hour of trial, and gives the reason for the forewarning: that the disciples, told in advance, might not despair of salvation, but doing penitence be restored. So the verse sets praise and descent side by side, a hymn sung on the way out to a garden.
31:
Clarke renders the warning as stumbling rather than offence, that they will all be made to stumble, forsake him and lose their confidence; and he develops the figure the prophecy supplies, since with the leader and guardian removed the whole flock is scattered and on the point of becoming a prey to ravenous beasts. Barnes supplies the occasion of the saying, which was Peter’s bold claim that he would die with him (John 13:37).

Ellicott calls the citation of Zechariah 13:7 every way suggestive, both because it shows where the Lord’s own thoughts had been dwelling that evening and because he did not merely quote the verse but led the disciples to dwell on the chapter, in which the smiting of the shepherd is bound up with the refining of the flock. He notes too that the saying corresponds in substance with what John reports in other words (John 16:32).

Henry sees a dismal scattering storm just arising, and names what the disciples would lack: they would be so frightened by the sufferings that they would not have the courage to cleave to him. Gill places the words on the road, noting that they were spoken either before the company left the house or as they were going along toward Olivet, so that the warning fell on the very way into the night of trial.

Calvin addresses a difference among the Gospels, that what Matthew and Mark extend to all the disciples Luke reports as spoken to Peter. His solution is that Christ spoke to them in the person of one man, the one who needed admonishing more than all the rest, and who would afterwards need extraordinary consolation, so that having denied Christ he might not be altogether overwhelmed with despair. Wesley states the plain sense without the figure, that something will happen to him which will occasion their falling into sin by forsaking him. The forewarning is therefore not pitched to crush the men who heard it but to keep them, when it came true, from reading their own collapse as the end of the matter.
32:
Gill gathers the comfort of the verse into a sequence, that though their shepherd should be apprehended, condemned and crucified, smitten with death and laid in the grave, yet he should rise again; and though they should be scattered abroad, yet they should be gathered together again by him. Clarke puts the same assurance as an instruction: do not lose your confidence, for though he will appear for a time to be wholly left to wicked men and brought under the power of death, he will rise again and triumph over all their enemies and his own. Barnes reads the promise as serving two purposes at once, given to encourage and support them and also as an indication where he might afterwards be found, since he would meet them all in Galilee, as in the event he did (Mark 16:7; Matthew 28:16). Clarke keeps the shepherd figure running through both verses: though the shepherd has been smitten and the sheep scattered, the shepherd shall revive, collect the scattered flock, and go before them. Gill puts it in the same terms, that the sheep should be gathered again by their good shepherd, who after his rising would appear to them, be at the head of them and go before them.

Ellicott enters a sober observation about how the promise was received, or rather not received. These words appear to have fallen at the time unheeded and to have been rapidly forgotten, since no expectation of a resurrection is traceable in the disciples’ after conduct. The comfort was given before it could be understood, which is one reason the women at the tomb were not expecting anything.

Calvin reads the verse out of Zechariah, following the prophet’s own sequence. After foretelling the scattering, Zechariah goes on to treat of the restoration of the Church, precisely so that the godly should not be overwhelmed with despair; and Calvin draws from it the assurance that matters here, that God does not cease to recognise as his own those who are for a time driven out and scattered.

Wesley reduces the whole to a sentence that answers the fear the previous verse raised: though you forsake me, I will not for this forsake you. The promise is lodged exactly where it is most needed, between the prophecy of the scattering and its fulfilment a few hours later, so that the men who were about to fail had already been told where to find him afterwards.
33:
Barnes begins with a textual correction that changes the sense of the boast: the word men is wrongly inserted, and Peter meant the disciples, so that he is setting himself against his colleagues rather than against the world. He then traces the confidence to three roots, that it was entirely characteristic of the man, that it sprang from true love to Jesus, and that it sprang equally from too much reliance on his own strength and from ignorance of himself. Robertson renders the verb as made to stumble and marks it a volitive future, and notices what Peter has passed over: he ignored the prophecy of the resurrection altogether, being intent on showing that he was superior to all the rest.

Gill explains why the boast came from this disciple and not another, since Peter was always a forward man, free to speak his mind, and often the mouth of the rest; so his words spoke for more than himself even as they singled him out. Ellicott notes a harmonistic difficulty in the placing, Matthew and Mark setting the boast after the company left the room where Luke and John set it before, and judges this an example of the natural dislocation that attends any report of rapid events.

Clarke turns the verse into a portrait of presumption and states it as a maxim. The presumptuous person imagines he can do everything and can do nothing, promises everything and performs nothing; and the strength of pride is only for a moment. His conclusion is the sentence that gives the scene its sting, that there is nothing we know so little of as ourselves.

Calvin is careful to credit Peter with sincerity before faulting him. He uses no hypocrisy but speaks with sincere affection; it is a false confidence in his own virtue that carries him away into foolish boasting, and he is justly reproved because he had not been sufficiently careful to examine himself. The event showed that he promised more for himself than he was able to accomplish. What the verse records, then, is not a lie but a miscalculation, and the warmest affection proving no safeguard where self-knowledge is missing.
34:
Barnes reconciles the Gospels on the signal. Mark and Luke add that the cock would crow twice, and he explains the usage: the bird crows about midnight and again at break of day, the latter being what was familiarly called the cock-crowing (Mark 13:35). Lightfoot harmonises the accounts by taking the phrase to mean within the time of cock-crowing rather than before any crowing at all, which squares Matthew with John 13:38. Wesley dates it more exactly still, at before three in the morning, the usual hour, while noting that one cock was heard to crow once after Peter’s first denial.

Clarke presses how much the warning specifies, and the specificity is the point. This is not a gradual falling away but something Peter will do this very night; and it is not merely a forsaking but a denial that he has, or ever had, any knowledge of the man he is speaking to. Gill notes the solemn prefix, the Amen that Christ puts before the sentence as marking a certain truth, so that nothing in the prediction is offered tentatively.

Ellicott argues from the agreement of the records that the prediction stands beyond the shadow of a doubt, all four Evangelists reporting it, and calls the prevision essentially superhuman. He adds the detail that makes it more searching rather than merely accurate: to the sin thus foretold there was attached a penalty already published, against whoever should deny the Son before men, so that Peter had been told in advance both what he would do and what it would cost.

Cyril of Jerusalem stays with the formula rather than the prophecy, setting this solemn assurance beside the one given to the penitent thief, that this day he should be with him in paradise (Luke 23:43). The same words of sovereign certainty serve in one place to foretell a fall and in the other to seal a salvation. What the verse fixes is the night, the number and the signal, and its fulfilment to the letter was what afterwards broke Peter to a saving repentance.
35:
Gill marks the manner of the reply from Mark, that Peter spake the more vehemently, his spirit raised to a greater pitch and his protest cast in stronger terms than before. Robertson notes the double negative in the Greek, the strongest form of denial available, and judges the speech fairly: it was a noble speech and meant well, even as the boast is made still stronger than it was a moment earlier. He adds what the others were doing while Peter spoke, that they were undoubtedly embarrassed by the exchange and lightheartedly joined in the same profession.

Barnes states the outcome against which the vow has to be read. They all said it, and they all fled at the approach of danger, practically denying that they knew him (Matthew 26:56); and he glosses the word itself, to deny being to disown connection with him or any acquaintance with him at all. Clarke diagnoses what went wrong in the reasoning rather than in the affection: Peter does not take the warning, trusting instead in the warm, sincere attachment he feels at that moment, without considering that it must speedily fail unless supported by the power of God.

Ellicott is careful to say that Peter was not alone in the resolve, and finds a precedent for it. Thomas had spoken much the same words before (John 11:16), and all of them felt as if they were prepared to face death. His explanation of why is worth keeping: to these men Christ had been not merely righteous but good and kind, and so for him they even dared to die, which is the distinction Paul draws about dying for a good man rather than a just one (Romans 5:7).

Wesley notices what Christ does not say, and makes the silence the point: such was the tenderness of our Lord that he would not aggravate their sin by making any reply. The vow was sincere and the collapse was certain, and he let both stand without a word. Gill observes that the rest followed where Peter led, all of them saying the same in their turn, so that the whole company was committed to a promise none of them would keep.
36:
Robertson and Barnes locate the place, an enclosed olive orchard beyond the brook Kidron at the foot of Olivet (John 18:1), where ancient olives were still standing in their own day; the name means oil-press, and Clarke derives it from the words for press and oil. Jerome gives a different interpretation of it, the rich valley, and notes that there the Lord prayed alone for all. Calvin brings in Luke’s detail that Christ came there as he was wont, and draws the inference that matters: he went to a known place not to hide but, as if he had made an assignation with his enemies, to present himself to death (John 18:2), which Calvin treats as a further proof of his obedience.

Hilary reports the use some had made of the sorrow that follows, reading it as proof that fear of death assailed the Son of God and therefore that he was a creature made from nothing, an inference he resists. Ambrose answers it by distinguishing within Christ rather than denying the grief: he is sorrowful, yet not himself but his soul, for he took upon him my soul and my body. Jerome puts the same distinction in terms of what can and cannot suffer, the impassible Deity remaining while the Son of God suffered actually in respect of that part of him which could suffer. Augustine simply appeals to the record, the Evangelists standing as witnesses that he had a true body and a true soul.

Chrysostom notices the arrangement of the garden, that Christ prayed apart and so teaches us to study quiet and retirement for our prayers, and that he took only the three lest the rest be cast down by what they saw. Origen reads the sorrow as bounded rather than endless, hearing in the words that his soul was sorrowful unto death a grief whose beginnings only are in him, not to endure for ever but to be ended when, dying for sin, he should die also to all sorrow.

Henry names the moment for what it is, the beginning of sorrows, and finds in it the prophecy of the sword awaking against the man that was God’s fellow. What the garden sets before all of them is a real and not a feigned anguish, borne by a true human soul, and sought out in the place and the company of prayer.
37:
Barnes and Robertson note which men were taken and why it matters. Peter, James and John had been the three favoured at the raising of Jairus’s daughter (Luke 8:51) and at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1), and are here chosen out of the chosen again; Robertson says plainly what they were taken for, to share the agony of soul and to give him some human sympathy. Gill offers a second reason, that they were the strongest and best able to bear the shocking sight, and a third that turns on their history: having witnessed his glory on the mount they were very proper persons to witness his abasement, so that the one sight might interpret the other. Clarke puts the same thought the other way round, that they might contemplate this agony in the light of the glory they had already seen.

On the words for the sorrow the expositors reach for stronger language than the English carries. Barnes observes that the second term is much stronger than the first. Clarke renders the pair as an exquisite sorrow, such as dissolves the natural vigour and threatens to separate soul from body.

Wesley probes the cause as far as he thinks reverence allows, and no further. The anguish came probably from feeling the arrows of the Almighty stick fast in his soul, while God laid on him the iniquities of us all; and he breaks off with a question rather than an answer, asking who can tell what painful and dreadful sensations were then impressed on him by the immediate hand of God. The word, he adds, signifies to be penetrated with the most exquisite sorrow.

Calvin reads the moment as a change in the nature of the trial. Here is the true test of virtue, since Christ now fights face to face with temptation, and the weakness of the flesh, which was formerly concealed, shows itself. God had tried his Son before by preparatory exercises; now he brings on the great contest, and what had been borne hitherto in anticipation now has to be borne in fact.
38:
