Barnes takes the words of the human nature, the soul being much and deeply affected, and explains the idiom in the second clause, where the sufferings of death stand for extreme and indescribable anguish: the sense is that his sorrows are so great that under their burden he is ready to die. Clarke renders it as being surrounded with exceeding sorrow, the soul so dissolved in grief that unless speedy succour be given to the body, death must be the result.

Robertson glosses the request as keeping awake rather than keeping vigil in any formal sense, and reads the plea for what it costs to make: Jesus pleaded for a bit of human sympathy as he wrestled with his Father, and it did not seem too much to ask of men who had just vowed to die with him. Ellicott says the same in his own terms, that the infinite sadness of that hour leads the Master to crave sympathy from the three, and adds what the watching could and could not supply. They might not fully see or hear the throes of the agony; it would be something to know that they were at least watching with him, sharers in that awful vigil.

Calvin explains why the sorrow was spoken of at all rather than borne in silence. Christ communicates it to them in order to arouse them to sympathy, and so that they might afterwards be the more ashamed of their carelessness. On the phrase itself he is blunt: it expresses a deadly wound of grief, as if he had said that he fainted or was half dead, and he compares Jonah’s answer that he was sorrowful even unto death (Jonah 4:9).

Calvin also registers a disagreement with his predecessors on this verse, noting that some of the ancient writers handled the passage with too much fear of admitting that Christ truly grieved. His own reading declines that caution, and the plain sense of the sentence supports him: the sorrow is neither feigned nor slight but reaches to death, and the only thing asked of his friends is that they stay awake beside him.
39:
Origen guards the mystery by locating the prayer precisely. Christ prays not according to his divine and impassible Substance but according to his human and weak nature, for in taking upon him the nature of human flesh he fulfilled all the properties of it. Augustine reads the same words as a pattern offered to us: man, behold thyself in me, that thou canst will somewhat apart of thyself, and then subordinate it, as the second clause does. Hilary proposes a distinctive reading in which the petition is not for himself at all, Christ praying not from fear but that the cup, as it is drunk by him, may also be drunk by his disciples without fear of death. Leo makes the words the health of the whole body, instruction to the faithful which crowns the martyr.

Barnes draws the doctrine of the atonement out of the refusal rather than the request. The fact that these sufferings were not removed shows that it was not consistent with the justice of God that men should be saved without the awful sufferings of such an atonement; and when Jesus speaks of his own will he expresses what human nature, in view of such great sufferings, would naturally desire. Ellicott connects the prayer to the statement that he learned obedience by the things he suffered (Hebrews 5:8), and reads the conditional clause as recognising the natural and necessary limits of our Lord’s humanity. Robertson marks the speed of the surrender, that he instantly gave his will over to the Father’s and drank the cup to the full, and judges that here Jesus won the power to go on to Calvary.

Calvin gives the fullest treatment, and begins by admitting the prayer is abrupt, like a vessel tossed by tempests: the strength and violence of grief suddenly drew this word from his mouth, to which he immediately added a correction. Against those who deny that Christ feared he points to the bloody sweat (Luke 22:44), since that mortal sweat could only have proceeded from fearful and unusual horror, when he saw the wrath of God exhibited to him and himself charged with the sins of the whole world.

Calvin then answers the harder question the verse raises, how two wills can be named without conflict. In Christ the divine and the human will differed from each other without any contest, as discordant musical notes may be sounded together and produce a harmony. Wesley adds the outcome from Hebrews, that he was heard in the thing he feared, God taking away the terror and severity of that inward conflict. The Son of God, truly man, shrinks from death and yields perfectly, and the yielding is what the prayer is for.
40:
Barnes corrects the reading most people bring to the scene. The sleep was just the reverse of stupid indifference; it was proof of their great attachment and their deep sympathy, since Luke says plainly that they slept for sorrow. He supports this with medical testimony that profound sleep follows great grief, instancing mothers at the death of a child and criminals on the eve of execution. Ellicott supplies the other half of the explanation, that it was now near the dawning of the day and their eyes had not closed in sleep for four-and-twenty hours.

The reproof falls on one man in particular. Clarke frames it as a question put to Peter’s own profession: is this the way you testify your affectionate attachment to me, when you all said you were ready to die with me, and cannot watch one hour? He notes a manuscript variant that makes the reproach singular, couldst thou not. Ellicott observes that Mark individualises it further, addressing him as Simon rather than Peter, and draws the contrast sharply: he had boasted of his readiness to do great things, and could not so much as rouse himself to watch for one hour. Robertson hears in the sentence a tone of sad disappointment and says that every word struck home, noting that the single hour measures the time which had passed since their Master left them.

Calvin takes the measure of what the failure cost. It was a bitter aggravation of his sufferings that even these forsook him; and although he did not need the assistance of anyone, yet since he had voluntarily taken upon him our infirmities, the indifference of those he had selected as his companions added a heavy and distressing burden to his grief.

Calvin also draws from the coming and going a rule about the rhythm of prayer. Believers are not required to be so constant in prayer as never to cease; following the example of Christ here, they continue their prayers as far as their infirmity allows, then cease for a short time, and immediately after drawing breath return to God. The gentle question to Peter, who had boasted so loudly an hour before (v.33), is at once a reproof and a warning of the larger failure now a few hours off.
41:
Barnes identifies the temptation in view, which is the coming trial of their faith in the rejection and death of Jesus. He explains why that would try them specifically: they had cherished the belief that he was to establish a kingdom while he lived, and the cross would overturn it. He is careful about what the exhortation is for, that it was not intended as an apology for their sleeping but to rouse them to be on guard, lest the weakness of human nature prove insufficient for what was coming.

Ellicott traces the afterlife of the first word, which became the watchword of the early disciples (1 Corinthians 16:13; Colossians 4:2; 1 Peter 5:8) and left its mark even in the names Gregory and Vigilantius, the watcher. He also hears a tenderness in the warning, since the Master recognises the element of good in them, their readiness to go with him to prison or to death, even while naming the war of flesh against spirit (Galatians 5:17).

Clarke puts the practical argument as a comparison from the lesser to the greater: if you cannot endure a little fatigue when there is no suffering, how will you do when the temptation comes? Watch, that you be not taken unawares, and pray, that when it comes you may be enabled to bear it. Robertson connects the words to the petition about temptation in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13), which he takes to be asking not to be led into it. Wesley reads the whole as remarkable for its manner, how gentle a rebuke and how kind an apology, especially at a moment when our Lord’s own mind was so weighed down with sorrow.

Calvin draws out the logic by which weakness becomes a reason for prayer rather than for despair. The manner of resistance enjoined here is not to draw courage from reliance on our own strength but, on the contrary, from a conviction of our weakness to ask arms and strength from the Lord. He notes the balance Christ keeps, giving them the praise of a willing spirit so that their weakness may not throw them into despair, and yet urging prayer because they are not sufficiently endued with the power of the Spirit. The general rule he derives is that we must keep diligent watch by prayer, since we do not yet possess the power in such measure as not to fall frequently through the weakness of the flesh; and the promise attached to it is that all who, being earnest in prayer, perseveringly oppose the slothfulness of the flesh will be victorious.
42:
Ellicott detects a slight change of tone between this prayer and the last. It is as though the conviction that it was not possible for the cup to pass away had come with fuller clearness before his mind, and he was learning to accept it; so that he finds the answer to the former prayer in the continuance, and not the removal, of the bitter agony. Ellicott places here Luke’s great drops of blood and the strengthening angel (Luke 22:43–44). Calvin reads the same development: Christ no longer asks to have the cup removed but, leaving out that prayer, insists rather on obeying the purpose of God, the first encounter with temptation having animated him to approach death with greater confidence.

Barnes devotes a long treatment to the bloody sweat, defending the fact against sceptics with parallels from Aristotle and Diodorus and from Voltaire’s account of Charles IX, whose blood oozed out of all his pores. He then answers why the divine nature did not minister strength to the human, which is the question the strengthening angel raises. Christ came to be a perfect example of a holy man, and so submitted to the common conditions of humanity, that he should suffer as other men suffer and be strengthened as other men are strengthened (Hebrews 1:14).

On the cause of the agony itself Barnes declines to dogmatise, and says why: where the Scriptures are silent about the cause, it does not become us confidently to express an opinion. The most he will venture is a rush of feeling from every quarter, the sufferings of the atonement pouring together upon him at once.

Clarke takes the words as evidence that the atonement was both real and free. It was his humanity alone that could suffer, and if it did not appear that he felt these sufferings there would be a presumption that he had not suffered and so had made no atonement; and had he not appeared perfectly resigned, the sacrifice could not have been a free-will but a constrained offering. The movement from asking that the cup pass (v.39) to accepting that it may not therefore traces, in Christ’s own words, the progress of an obedience that is neither feigned nor forced.
43:
Gill describes what had happened in the interval, that they were roused and awaked in some measure by what he had said to them, but no sooner was he gone than they fell asleep again. Robertson parses the construction as a periphrastic past perfect, their eyes having been weighted down with sleep and still being so, and connects the drowsiness with an earlier occasion, since the same thing had happened on the Mount of Transfiguration (Luke 9:32).

Ellicott reads the manner of Christ’s return rather than the fact of their sleep. What brings him back is the craving for human sympathy in that hour of awful agony; and this time he does not rouse them or speak to them, but looks on them sorrowfully, and they meet his gaze with bewildered and stupefied astonishment, not knowing what to answer him (Mark 14:40). Clarke raises a question the others leave unasked, whether there was anything preternatural in the heaviness, and whether the powers of darkness had some influence in weighing down their eyes at the very moment they should have been watching.

Calvin works from the cause Luke assigns, which is sorrow. This drowsiness arose neither from excessive eating and drinking nor from gross stupidity, but rather from immoderate grief; and he draws from that the more alarming conclusion, that we perceive the more clearly how strong is the tendency of our flesh to indifference, since even dangers lead us to forgetfulness of God. He then shows how the adversary profits either way: if we dread no danger he intoxicates and drowns us in security, and if we experience the fear and sorrow which ought to arouse us to pray, he overwhelms our senses instead.

Calvin also measures the aggravation in who these men were and when it happened. The disciples fall asleep again almost at the very moment of having been sharply reproved; and these are not the whole body but the three whom Christ had selected to be his chief companions, the flower of them. Against that he sets the example of the one man awake, drawing the rule that we must not be discouraged or grow weary in praying if we do not immediately obtain our wishes.
44:
Gill explains the withdrawal in practical terms, that he went some little distance from them, they being so overpowered with sleep that he could have no conversation with them. Clarke reaches for the Pauline parallel, since Paul besought the Lord thrice that his affliction might depart from him (2 Corinthians 12:8), and draws the inference that thrice repeating the same petition argues deep earnestness of soul.

Ellicott makes the repetition itself the matter worth noticing, and distinguishes two kinds of it. The fact is suggestive as indicating that there is a repetition in prayer which indicates not formalism but intensity of feeling. Lower forms of sorrow may, as it were, play with grief and vary the forms of its expression, where the deepest and sharpest agony is content to fall back upon the iteration of the self-same words.

That distinction is what separates this threefold prayer from the vain repetitions Christ had himself warned against (Matthew 6:7). The words are the same because the burden is the same, and because there is nothing further to say about it. The prayer was answered, not by the removal of the cup, but by the strength to drink it; and the man who rose from the third repetition went to meet the betrayer with composure.
45:
The apparent contradiction with the command to rise and go a verse later (v.46) is the difficulty here, and Augustine’s solution is the most cited. Drawing on Mark’s addition that it is enough (Mark 14:41), he takes the Lord to have been silent for some time after telling them to sleep on, allowing them to do so, and then after an interval to have roused them. Barnes prefers to read the clause as a question, asking whether they sleep now and take their rest, and whether this is a time to give themselves to sleep, which he supports from Luke’s why sleep ye. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson allow instead a mournful irony. Calvin is decisive for irony with a sting in it: having hitherto wasted his words on them, he will now come to exhort them, but whatever permission he may give them to rest, the enemies will not allow it and will compel them to watch against their will.

Hilary reads the threefold finding of them asleep as a history of the Church, rebuked after the resurrection, visited by the Spirit, and at last given rest at Christ’s glorious coming. Origen distinguishes this permitted rest from the earlier heavy-eyed sleep, allowing that the soul, unable to sustain a continual energy, may blamelessly admit some relaxations.

Chrysostom attends to the two halves of the announcement. That he is delivered into the hands of sinners shows this was the work of their wickedness and not that he was guilty of any crime, while that the hour is at hand points to divine interference, the timing being not theirs. Jerome adds what Christ does with the hour, going forth undaunted and offering himself voluntarily to be sacrificed.

Ellicott dates the change of tone by the arrival of the men, noting that it was not until after these words had been spoken that the Traitor and his companions were seen actually approaching. Robertson reads the same turn in Christ himself: the Master’s time of weakness is past and he is prepared to face the worst, having won the victory without his disciples’ aid. Cyril of Jerusalem supplies the reason the victory took that form, that he came to his passion willingly, lest the whole world should perish in its sins. The verse therefore marks the hinge of the night, the prayer finished and the hour struck.
46:
Gill insists the summons is not what it first sounds like. It is not to run away from the enemy but to meet him; Christ was now rid of his fears and free from those agonies and dreadful apprehensions, and the rising signifies his willingness to be apprehended, and to suffer and die in the room of his people. Barnes and Ellicott read the second clause the same way, holding that it involves no suggestion of flight but rather a call to confront the danger. Clarke puts the willingness into Christ’s own voice: he goes willingly to meet the death their malice designs him, and through it to provide for the life of the world.

Robertson notices which verb is used of the betrayer’s approach, the same word John the Baptist had used of the kingdom drawing near (Matthew 3:2). He is candid about what the text does not tell us, that we cannot know whether Jesus heard the approach, or saw the lights, or simply felt the proximity of the traitor.

Calvin makes the verse the seal of what the praying accomplished. By these words he declares that, after having prayed, he was furnished with new arms. He had formerly been sufficiently voluntary as to dying, but when he came to the point he had a hard struggle with the weakness of the flesh; now, by prayer having obtained new strength from heaven (Hebrews 5:7), the trembling is allayed and the fear subdued, so that he not only does not retire or conceal himself but cheerfully advances to death.

Wesley catches the bearing in which he goes, and it is the note the whole arrest sounds: with what composure does he go forth to meet the traitor, plainly showing his superiority over them, and even then leading as it were captivity captive. The measure of the victory won in the garden is the distance between the man who fell on his face pleading that the cup might pass and the man who now stands up and walks toward the men who have come for him.
47:
The phrase naming the betrayer carries the weight of the verse. Robertson says the very horror of the thing is thus emphasised, that one of the chosen twelve apostles should do this dastardly deed. Clarke measures the descent: he who a little before had been one of the leaders of the flock of Christ is now become the leader of ruffians and murderers, which he calls a terrible fall.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson identify the force from John’s fuller account (John 18:3). It included the Roman cohort sent by Pilate to prevent a tumult, armed with swords, together with the temple officers carrying clubs, and they came with lanterns and torches although it was near the full moon of the Passover. Ellicott explains why they went to that particular garden, since it was known to Judas as one at least of our Lord’s chosen resorts (John 18:2).

Calvin reads the size of the band as evidence against the men who assembled it. Christ was not dragged to death by external violence, except so far as wicked men carried into execution the secret purpose of God; and the disproportion of the force betrays a bad conscience, since the divine power of Christ, which they had been compelled to feel by numerous proofs, inwardly tormented them. Henry draws the application from what Christ is left without: as a sacrifice for sins he stood thus abandoned, and in this he was made a curse for us. On the flight that follows (v.56) Henry is willing to call it both things at once, their sin, with unkindness and unfaithfulness in it, and also a part of Christ’s suffering, to be thus deserted. Of the betrayal itself he says that no enemies are so much to be abhorred as those professed disciples who betray Christ with a kiss.

Leo lifts the scene to the doctrine it serves, that among all the works of God’s mercy none is more wondrous than that Christ was crucified for the world, in which the Catholic Faith maintains the two Natures to have met in our Redeemer. Origen brings it uncomfortably forward, finding that Jesus is betrayed into the hands of sinners even now, when those who seem to believe in him continue to sin while they have him in their hands.
48:
Gill explains why a sign was needed at all, and gives three reasons. It was night, so that Judas himself might not be able to discern him readily; Christ and his apostles might be clothed alike, so that a mistake could easily be made; and the Roman soldiers in the party might never have seen him. Barnes adds the conclusion that follows, that Judas, being well acquainted with him, agreed to designate him by one of the tokens of friendship to prevent the possibility of mistake. Barnes also recalls from John what happened when the band arrived, that at the words I am he they went backward and fell to the ground (John 18:6).

Clarke is vehement about the coldness of the arrangement, calling the apostate coolly deliberate, deeply hypocritical and diabolically malicious. He reaches for a precedent and finds it insufficient: Joab inquired tenderly after the health of Amasa while thrusting him through with his sword, and the disciple here vastly outdoes his master. Robertson notes from Mark’s pluperfect that the sign had been arranged before the party arrived at the garden, and that Judas chose the kiss because it was a common greeting, intending to give it fervently.

Calvin probes why the traitor needed a sign rather than simply pointing. He has no doubt Judas was restrained, either by reverence for our Lord or by shame for his crime, from venturing openly to avow himself as one of the enemies. The instruction to hold him fast he traces to a different motive, conjecturing that Judas recollected the numerous proofs by which Christ had formerly attested his divine power, and feared what might happen once hands were laid on him.

That combination is what Calvin finds hardest to credit, and he names it astonishing madness: either to attempt to conceal himself by frivolous hypocrisy when he came into the presence of the Son of God, or to oppose the tricks and dexterity of men to his boundless power. The sign is the perversion of a token of love into an instrument of arrest, and the warning attached to it shows a man who believed in the power he was selling and went through with the sale regardless.
49:
Gill notes the staging of the approach, that Judas went on ahead of the band so that it might not be thought he came with them. Barnes explains the greeting, which is a word meaning to rejoice or to have cause of joy, and expresses the gladness one friend has on meeting another, especially after an absence — which is what makes its use here grotesque. The title is Rabbi, and the kiss was the common salutation of friends.

Lightfoot adds a point of custom that sharpens the question of what the gesture meant. It was not unusual for a master to kiss his disciple, but for a disciple to kiss his master was more rare; and he leaves the inference open, asking whether Judas did this under pretence of respect or out of open contempt and derision. Robertson weighs the verb instead, which is intensive and means he kissed him fervently, and calls it the most terrible instance of the profuse kisses of an enemy (Proverbs 27:6). The same verb is used of the sinful woman at Christ’s feet (Luke 7:38), of the father embracing the prodigal (Luke 15:20), and of the Ephesian elders parting from Paul (Acts 20:37), so that the warmth of the gesture is not incidental to the treachery but the vehicle of it.

Calvin reads the words as feigned compassion rather than mere cover. Judas, as if trembling for his Master’s danger, pretended by these words to have some feeling of concern for him, and Mark’s repeated address he takes for the speech of a man who spoke from strong feeling. He also notes the timing of the kiss, since Judas had left Christ only a little before, so that this reads as a last salute to his Master; thus he excels the rest in the appearance of affection.

What Calvin finds most revealing is the self-deception underneath. Though he was impressed with the majesty of Christ, still the devil so fascinated his mind that he felt assured his treachery was concealed; and how little he gained by the deception is evident from the reply he received. The man who had eaten at that table greets his Master with the warmest tokens of love at the moment of handing him over, convinced the disguise was holding.
50:
The word of address is not the warm one. Barnes explains that the Greek has two words rendered friend in English, one implying affection and the other not, and that it is the latter here, the same used of the disaffected labourer (Matthew 20:13) and of the guest without a wedding garment (Matthew 22:12). Clarke renders it companion, and Ellicott comrade or mate, a term such as fellow-soldiers or sailors used of each other.

Robertson turns to the question itself and follows Deissmann, who showed from a first-century Syrian tablet that the phrase was current coin in the language of the people, and so reads it as a sharp imperative rather than a puzzled inquiry: do your errand. Barnes takes it as designed to fill the mind of Judas with the consciousness of his crime, and by a striking question to compel him to think of what he was doing. Clarke imagines the sting it carried, that surely one who had so long been his companion is not come against his Lord, Teacher and Friend.

Calvin will not have it read as irony but as a grave charge. Christ charges him with ingratitude, that from being an intimate who sat at his table he had become a traitor, as had been predicted in the psalm (Psalms 41:9). He then widens the charge into a standing warning for the Church, since this evil, which Christ once sustained in his own person, is an evil to which the Church will always be exposed, that of cherishing traitors in her bosom; and the conclusion he draws is personal, that we who are his disciples ought to worship God with sincerity, so that no one give him a traitor’s kiss.

Wesley admires the bearing throughout: with what composure does he go forth to meet the traitor, with what calmness receive that malignant kiss, with what dignity deliver himself into the hands of his enemies, even then leading as it were captivity captive. Gill and Clarke note what the sequence shows about the submission, since hands were laid on him only after the band had been struck down by his word (John 18:6). The reply is therefore a reproach, an appeal to the man’s conscience, and a display of composure in one who could have left at any moment.
51:
The swordsman is Peter, named only by John (John 18:10), and the man struck is Malchus, whose ear Christ healed (Luke 22:51). Robertson explains why the other Evangelists leave the name out, which was for prudential reasons while Peter was still living, and judges that he aimed at the man’s head and not his ear. Barnes accounts for the weapons, the apostles having provided two swords (Luke 22:38) of the kind carried in seasons of danger against robbers. Chrysostom reads the earlier instruction about buying a sword (Luke 22:36–38) as serving a different purpose altogether, given not to arm them but to assure them that he was to be betrayed, and he supposes the two swords at hand were for the paschal lamb.

Clarke marks the healing as another miracle and a striking proof of the Divinity of Christ, since restoring a severed ear required unlimited power. Jerome turns to the wounded man’s name, since Malchus means one who should have been king and is instead made the slave of the ungodliness of the Priests, losing his right ear so that he might hear only the worthlessness of the letter. Hilary and Origen read the cut ear in the same direction, as the disobedient hearing of a people who were the slaves of the priesthood.

Augustine weighs Peter’s act carefully on both sides. He used the sword without the command or sanction of any superior or legitimate authority, and yet he sinned not through hardened ferocity but through a warmth of spirit capable of good, as Moses did in smiting the Egyptian. Leo explains why no such defence was permitted, since Christ gives licence to their fury against him, lest by putting off the triumph of his glorious Cross the dominion of the Devil should be made longer.

Calvin draws the lesson about zeal that outruns its orders. We are much more courageous and ready for fighting than for bearing the cross; and Peter did not wait till he was commanded or permitted to strike, but inconsiderately proceeded to unlawful violence. Their valour is justly condemned because they improperly attempt more than the calling of God commands, the rule being that no man shall move a finger except so far as God commands. The blow sprang from love and was still rash, and the healing of the wound it made rebukes the violence and shows the power in the same act.
52:
Barnes offers three possible senses and prefers to read the saying as a caution to Peter, whose unseasonable and imprudent defence might be the occasion of his own destruction, since those who took the sword perished by it; he suspects the words were already a proverb. Clarke reads it as caution and prophecy together, a declaration about the Jewish and Roman states, both of which took the sword against Christ and both of which perished by it. Robertson states it flatly as a principle, that offensive war is here given condemnation, since the sword calls for the sword.

Ellicott guards against over-reading. The words are obviously not a general rule declaring the unlawfulness of all warfare, but are limited in their range by the occasion, resistance at that moment being a fight not for God but against him. He nevertheless draws a narrower inference and keeps it: in whatever other cause it may be lawful to use carnal weapons, it is not wise or right to draw the sword for Christ and his Truth (2 Corinthians 10:4).

Augustine supplies the distinction the saying turns on, that a man uses the sword in the condemned sense who, without the command or sanction of any superior or legitimate authority, arms himself against another man’s life. Hilary argues from the plain facts that not all who use a sword literally die by one, so that the meaning must concern those who use it for the promotion of crime. Leo gives the reason no defence could be allowed here, that it was contrary to the sacrament of our redemption that he who had come to die for all should refuse to be apprehended.

Calvin works the question out most carefully, taking the saying to confirm the precept of the Law which forbids private individuals to use the sword. He then separates a civil court from the court of conscience: a man who repels a robber will not be liable to public punishment, because the laws arm him, while lawful self-defence requires that he first lay aside excessive wrath, hatred and desire of revenge. Because this scarcely ever happens, Christ properly reminds his people of the general rule, that they should entirely abstain from using it. Against those who would wrest the sword out of the hands of judges Calvin is equally firm, since magistrates are God’s ministers, to whom this very power is expressly ascribed.
53:
Gill begins with the one qualification the sentence needs, that it must be understood of Christ as man, since as God the angels were his own creatures and ministering servants and needed no asking for. Barnes identifies what Peter’s blow implied, a distrust of the protection of God; had rescue been proper, God could easily have furnished far more efficient aid than a sword, namely a mighty host of angels. On the numbers, Barnes notes that a legion was more than six thousand men and suggests the figure twelve was chosen with the apostles in view, and Clarke computes the whole at more than seventy-two thousand. Ellicott makes the same connection and sharpens the contrast: not twelve weak men, but twelve legions of the armies of the Lord of Hosts. Robertson recalls the precedent at Dothan, where Elisha’s servant was shown the horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:17).

Ellicott then notices something subtler in the wording, a strange and suggestive blending of the possible and the impossible. Could Christ have brought himself to utter that prayer, it would have been answered; but he could not so pray unless he knew it to be in harmony with his Father’s will, and he had been taught in that hour of agony that it was not. The adverb, Ellicott adds, means immediately, without a moment’s delay.

Calvin resolves the same difficulty by attending to the conditional form. Christ speaks conditionally, that he has a far better method of defending his life were it not that the will of the Father was opposed to it; and he refrained from presenting such a request because he knew it was contrary to the divine decree.

From that Calvin draws a doctrine he calls useful, that those who resort to unlawful means on the plea of necessity pour dishonour on God. Few look for the secret protection of God, forgetting the angels placed as guardians over them (Hebrews 1:14). What the verse establishes is that the submission was not weakness: with twelve legions instantly available for the asking, he did not ask.
54:
Gill puts the question in its plainest form, asking how the Scriptures which speak of Christ being taken and led as a lamb to the slaughter should have their accomplishment if angels had rescued him. Barnes names the purpose of the saying as well as its content, that the Scriptures which foretold his dying for the world must be accomplished, and that Christ said this to comfort his disciples, showing them his death was not a matter of surprise or disappointment to him. Clarke points to the chief prophecies in view, Psalms 22 and 69 and especially Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9:24–27, and draws from them that his captors had no power against him but what he permitted, and that he willingly gave himself into their hands.

Ellicott finds in the clause the source of the peace and calmness which had come to our Lord’s human soul out of the depths of its agony. All that was sharpest and most bitter was part of a pre-ordained discipline; not otherwise could the Scriptures be fulfilled, which had painted the picture of the ideal Sufferer not less vividly than that of the ideal Conqueror and King. It was meet, he concludes with Hebrews, that he too should be made perfect through sufferings (Hebrews 2:10). Robertson says the same more briefly, that Jesus sees clearly his destiny now that he has won the victory in Gethsemane.

Calvin asks why Christ should need a written word at all, and answers by distinguishing his own knowledge from his disciples’. For himself he required no Scripture to know the Father’s appointment; but because mortals do not know what God has determined until it be revealed by his word, Christ, with a view to his disciples, properly refers to the testimony which God had given of his will.

From this Calvin draws the general use, that Scripture is a sufficient bridle for subduing the rebellion of the flesh, because God points out to us what his will is for the very purpose of keeping us in subjection (Romans 15:4). The submission at the arrest is therefore obedience to a revealed necessity rather than a yielding to superior force, which is why the man who had sweated blood an hour earlier could now stand still and let it happen.
55:
Ellicott and Robertson correct the rendering, since the word is not thief but robber, the same used of Barabbas (John 18:40), meaning the brigand chieftain of a lawless band. Robertson draws out the irony that follows from it, that Christ will be crucified between two robbers and on the very cross planned for their leader. Barnes measures what the comparison cost him, adding not a little to the depth of his humiliation that he consented to be hunted down thus by wicked men and treated as if he had been the worst of mankind.

On the contrast Christ draws with his daily teaching, Ellicott notes that the sitting implied the position of a teacher more or less recognised, and that the statement looks beyond the few recent days to a ministry in Jerusalem which the first three Gospels pass over. Clarke keeps to the nearer reckoning, that every day for four days past they might have met with him in the temple.

Chrysostom explains why they had not. They did not lay hands on him in the temple because they feared the multitude; and so the Lord went forth to the garden that he might give them place and opportunity to take him. The conclusion he draws is the one the whole arrest supports, that if he had not suffered them of his own free choice they would never have had strength to take him. Jerome puts the absurdity of the armament in a sentence: it is folly to seek with swords and staves one who offers himself to your hands.

Calvin voices the expostulation as a question put to the men holding the weapons, what necessity there was for making such a display of arms, as if their object had been to overcome some robber. He then reads their own conduct against them, since though they had a traitor for their leader they approached him with trembling, which wounded their evil conscience. The manner of the seizure, by night and by stealth and with a cohort against an unarmed teacher, is itself the confession the words draw out.
56:
Gill, Barnes and Ellicott take the first clause as Christ’s own words rather than the Evangelist’s comment, following Mark’s report of them (Mark 14:49). Ellicott describes what is being claimed, that the betrayal and arrest were all working out a divine purpose and fulfilling the Scriptures in which that purpose had been shadowed forth, and Barnes lists the places: Genesis 3:15, Psalms 22 and 69, Isaiah 53, Daniel 9:24–26 and Zechariah 13:7. Calvin states the doctrine in its hard form. Whatever unbridled rage Satan and ungodly men are actuated by, the hand of God always prevails, so as to draw them reluctantly wherever he pleases. He then adds the limit that keeps it from excusing anyone, since God does not employ such men as his lawful ministers, and they are therefore not excusable.

On the flight Clarke laments without softening it: Jesus is abandoned by all, even zealous Peter and loving John being among the fugitives, and he asks whether a master was ever so served by his scholars. He then turns the question on his reader, asking whether there are not found among Christ’s disciples still persons who abandon him, his people, his cause and his truth.

Ellicott offers two mitigations without pretending they are a defence, the weariness and exhaustion which had overcome the disciples, and the fact that they had been told not to resist, so that flight might seem to them the only alternative left. Henry holds both judgments at once, calling the desertion their sin, with unkindness and unfaithfulness in it, and also a part of Christ’s suffering; and he finds the deeper sense in Isaiah, that Christ as the Saviour of souls stood thus alone and trod the wine-press alone (Isaiah 63:3).

Barnes and Ellicott both note the odd detail Mark alone preserves, of a young man with a linen cloth cast about his naked body who fled naked when they seized him (Mark 14:51), probably the owner of the garden or some friend of Jesus. The desertion fulfilled the prediction made on the road a few hours before (v.31) and the prophecy of the smitten Shepherd whose sheep are scattered, so that even this fell inside the purpose the first clause names.
57:
Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott account for a step Matthew omits, since John records that Jesus was first led to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas; they explain it as a mark of respect to the former high priest and as allowing time for the council to gather. Caiaphas held the office for that year, and Ellicott notes he was already committed to the policy of condemnation, having prophesied that it was expedient one man should die for the people (John 11:49–50).

Ellicott itemises the procedural violations, and they are not minor. It was against the rules of Jewish law to hold a session of the Sanhedrin for the trial of capital offences by night, and more so on the Passover night; the gathering was therefore an informal one, probably a packed meeting of those who were parties to the plot, with men like Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea not summoned. Only at daybreak did they transform themselves into a formal court (Luke 22:66).

Henry draws two lessons from the men in the courtyard and the man on trial. On Peter’s following afar off he is blunt, that to follow Christ afar off is to begin to go back from him. On Christ’s answer under oath he notices a change of practice: hitherto Jesus had seldom professed expressly to be the Christ, and now he would not omit to make an open confession of it, as an example and encouragement to his followers to confess him before men.

Calvin presses what is most disturbing about the scene, which is the standing of the men conducting it. Nowhere else than at Jerusalem was there at that time either a temple of God or lawful worship or the face of a Church, and yet all of them unite in conspiring to extinguish the only hope of salvation; Caiaphas was a figure of the only Mediator and those with him represented the whole Church of God, and they condemn the Redeemer. Calvin reads it as the rejected cornerstone (Psalms 118:22) and the stone of stumbling (Isaiah 8:14), and adds the comfort he finds in the foretelling: the Lord wisely made provision that such wickedness of men should not perplex believing souls.
58:
Gill reads the two halves of the sentence against each other: Peter’s following Christ showed love to him, and keeping at a distance, following afar off, betrayed fear. Barnes puts the same division more fully, that it evinced real attachment and a desire to be near him, and also fear respecting his personal safety, so that he kept just so far off as to be out of danger. Barnes then turns it into a measure for the reader, since many imitate Peter, afraid to follow the Saviour closely and keeping so far back that it is difficult to discern they are in the train at all; and we may measure our piety by our desire to be with him. Wesley compresses the whole into a sentence, that love constrained him to follow his Master and fear made him follow afar off.

Clarke names the moment for what it became, the beginning of his dreadful fall, and draws a rule of prudence from it. When a man is weak in faith and can as yet only follow Christ at a distance, he should avoid all dangerous places and the company of those most likely to prove a snare; and Clarke makes the counterfactual explicit, that had Peter not got to the high priest’s palace and sat down with the servants, he would not thus have denied his Lord. Wesley says the same of the company, unfit companions as the event showed.

Ellicott and Barnes explain how he got in at all, since John reports that admission came through another disciple known to the high priest; and Peter sat in the courtyard with the officers and slaves at a charcoal fire kindled against the chill of the early dawn. Robertson sums the man up in a phrase, more courageous than the rest and yet not courageous enough.

Ellicott probes the stated motive, which was to see the end. It was, he believes, more than a vague curiosity, and there was something of sorrowful anxiety in it; but there was no fervent devotion, no prayer for himself or his Master, only the fevered restlessness of uncertain expectation, so that all the natural instability of his character had free play with nothing to control it. That is the link back to the garden: the watchful prayer Christ had urged (v.41) was precisely what was missing when the testing came.
59:
Chrysostom describes what the assembly was pretending to be and what it actually was. This conventicle of ruffians sought to give their conspiracy the character of a legal trial, where it was entirely a scene of confusion and uproar, in truth nothing more than the anarchy of a den of robbers. Clarke states the inversion plainly, calling it a prostitution of justice, since they first resolve to ruin him and then seek the proper means of effecting it. Robertson identifies the particular impropriety, that judges have no right to be prosecutors, and least of all to seek after false witness and even to offer bribes to get it.

Ellicott reads the tense of the Greek as implying a continued process of seeking rather than a single attempt, and explains why the search was so laborious. The law required at least two witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6), examined separately; and the haste which marked all the proceedings had probably prevented previous concert among the men produced, so that they contradicted one another when questioned apart.

Calvin states the principle the whole proceeding violates. Nothing was farther from the design of the priests than to inquire into the cause, for they had previously resolved to put Christ to death and now sought only a pretext for oppressing him; and it is impossible that equity can have any place where an examination of the cause is not the first step. Verdict first and evidence afterwards is not a flawed trial but the absence of one.

Origen finds the failure of the witnesses turning into evidence of the opposite kind, a great testimony in favour of Jesus, that he had lived and taught so irreproachably that though they were many and crafty and wicked they could find no semblance of fault in him. Calvin reaches the same conclusion in stronger terms, that amidst the darkness of their rage the innocence of the Son of God shone so brightly that the devils themselves might know he died innocent. The court that would not examine the cause ended by acquitting him in the act of condemning him.
60:
Gill explains the finding of none as meaning none that were fit for their purpose, the difficulty being usefulness rather than supply. Barnes guards against a misreading of the council’s intent: we are not to suppose they wished the men to be false witnesses, since they were indifferent on that point provided they could succeed in condemning him. What defeated them was the nature of the testimony, since the men produced differed about facts, times and circumstances, as all false witnesses do, so that their witness agreed not together (Mark 14:56). Barnes adds the constraint that made this fatal, that the Jews did not dare to condemn him without conforming, in appearance at least, to the requirements of the law. Robertson puts it as an epigram: they found false witnesses in plenty, but not the false witness that would stand any sort of test.

Clarke draws out why this was bound to happen. It is the property of falsity to be ever inconsistent and to contradict itself, so that they could not find two consistent testimonies, without which the Jewish law did not permit any person to be put to death.

Clarke then reads the frustration as providence rather than luck. The hand of God was in this business, for the credit of Jesus and the honour of the Christian religion he would not permit him to be condemned on a false accusation; and so at last they were obliged to change their ground, and he is condemned on the very evidence of his own innocence, purity and truth.

Calvin defines the term the Evangelist uses with some care, since the appellation of false witnesses is applied not to those who contrive a lie that had no foundation but to those who calumniously pervert what was justly said and turn it into a crime. The temple-saying is his instance, where they put a wrong interpretation on his words (John 2:19). From the triviality of the charge Calvin infers how greatly the priests and scribes were blinded by their fury, since without any pretext they demand that Christ be put to death.
61:
Barnes and Robertson trace the charge to a real saying, spoken three years before, that if they destroyed this temple he would raise it up in three days (John 2:19), which John explains of the temple of his body. In the accusers’ hands it becomes a threat against the building in Jerusalem. Mark records that even so their witness did not agree together, so that this charge too failed the legal requirement.

Jerome defines the falsity precisely, and the definition is the key to the whole episode: a false witness is one who takes what is said in a different sense from that in which it was said. He then itemises the three alterations. Christ said destroy, not I will destroy, because it is unlawful to lay hands on ourselves, and they changed it to I can destroy. He said the temple of God meaning a living and breathing temple, and they applied it to the temple of stone. And he said he would raise it up, which they turned into building it again, as a mason might.

Robertson calls the result a pitiful perversion of what Jesus had said, and notes the irony that the men who misreported it were themselves the ones who destroyed the temple he had meant, and that he raised it again in three days as he had promised. Barnes observes that Mark records the testimony in a different form, as a claim to destroy a temple made with hands and build another made without hands, and suggests both forms were used during the trial, each Evangelist recording it as given at one point. Clarke draws the general warning from the particular case, that it is very easy, by means of a few small alterations, to render the most holy things and innocent persons odious to the world, and even to take away the life of the innocent.

Ellicott notices an oddity in the record, that the two Gospels which report the charge do not report the words in which it had its starting-point, and suggests what had revived the memory: the second cleansing of the Temple (Matthew 21:12) brought back to mind the first and the saying that accompanied it. Even then the testimony would not hold, there being still discrepancies as to time, place and the exact words which did not fit the established rules of evidence. Having failed to convict him of any deed, the court was left with nothing to do but interrogate the accused himself.
62:
Gill describes the manner of the question, that the high priest rose up from his seat in great wrath, partly vexed that they could get no better testimony and partly provoked by Christ’s contemptuous silence. Barnes explains why there was nothing to answer: Jesus knew the evidence did not even appear to amount to anything worth a reply. He reads the question as put in anger, since they had utterly failed in their proof and had no way left but to draw the charge from his own lips.

Ellicott dwells on what the question presupposes, namely a long-continued silence while witness after witness uttered their clumsy falsehoods. He records a scholar’s testimony that at the Oberammergau Passion-play this silence came upon him with a force he had never felt before, and traces in it a deliberate fulfilment of the prophecy that the servant opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7), echoed afterwards by Peter (1 Peter 2:23). On the grammar he suggests joining the clauses, so that the question asks whether he answers nothing to what these witness against him.

Calvin exposes the insinuation buried in the question. Caiaphas triumphs over him on account of his silence, as if he were struck dumb by being vanquished; and it is an instance of extreme wickedness that he implies Christ is not free from blame because witnesses speak against him. The unspoken argument is that they would not have appeared against him without good reason — as if Caiaphas did not know that these men had been procured by fraud.

Calvin then gives two reasons for the second silence that follows. Christ was again silent not only because the objection was frivolous, but because, having been appointed to be a sacrifice, he had thrown aside all anxiety about defending himself. That is the distinction the scene turns on: the silence was not the dumbness of a man overcome, as Caiaphas pretended, but the composure of one who had resolved not to keep a life he had come to lay down. Barnes makes the same point from the evidence rather than the motive, since a reply was owed only to a charge that amounted to something, and this one did not.
63:
Gill accounts for the silence just broken, that Christ knew it would signify nothing whatever he should say, the men being set upon his death, and so he quietly submits. Clarke marks why the adjuration changes matters. To this solemn charge Christ immediately replies, because he is now called on in the name of God to bear another testimony to the truth; and Clarke puts the motive positively, that he felt no disposition to continue silent when questioned concerning a truth for which he came into the world to shed his blood.

Ellicott shows how carefully the question was framed, skilfully worded so as to force upon our Lord the alternative either of denying what indeed he was, or of making a confession which would be treated as blasphemy; technically it was an oath of compurgation (Exodus 22:11; Numbers 5:19–22). Robertson names the impropriety in it, that Caiaphas put Jesus on oath in order to make him incriminate himself, a thing unlawful in Jewish jurisprudence, and notes the trap in the silence itself, since to refuse to answer would be tantamount to a denial. He draws an incidental inference about an earlier saying, that Christ cannot have been thinking of oaths in courts of justice when he prohibited swearing (Matthew 5:34), since he answers one here.

Calvin probes the bad faith of the form. Caiaphas examines the matter on oath as if he had been prepared to yield as soon as it was fully ascertained, while all the while his whole mind is filled with a malicious hatred. What he ought first to have inquired into was whether Christ truly was the Messiah, examining the signs; instead, having already determined to put him to death, he is satisfied with this pretence of sacrilege.

Calvin also draws a point of usage from the wording of the oath, inferring that it was at that time common among the Jews to bestow on the Messiah the title of Son of God, which they had learned from the predictions of Scripture. The discrimination in Christ’s conduct is what the verse exhibits: silent under calumny, he speaks when the question is who he is, knowing that the answer will seal the verdict.
64:
Gill and Barnes take the opening phrase as a form of assenting, equivalent to the plain I am that Mark records, and Robertson calls it a Greek affirmative reply. What follows is more than assent. Drawing on Daniel 7:13 and Psalms 110:1, Christ adds a prediction that reverses the positions in the room, and Robertson states the effect bluntly: he claims that the day will come when Jesus will be the Judge and Caiaphas the culprit.

Ellicott weighs the confession against any reduced estimate of Christ, and does not hedge. No words in the whole Gospel records are more decisive against the views of those who would see in our Lord only a great moral teacher, like Socrates, since at the very crisis of his history, when denial would have saved his life, he asserts a claim to be much more than this. Ellicott then adds the argument from the circumstances, that when men stand face to face with seeming failure and with death, dreams and delusive claims for the most part melt away; here claims that men have presumed to think delusive were strengthened and intensified, and that in the calmness of assured conviction.

Calvin draws the contrast between the two appearings. Christ affirms that he is the Son of God not for the purpose of avoiding death but rather of inflaming the rage of his enemies against him; and though now almost annihilated by his mean garb, he announces that at the proper time he will come with royal majesty, so that they may tremble before the Judge whom they now refuse to acknowledge. Wesley puts the same contrast in a sentence, that our Lord looked very unlike that person now, and that nothing could be more awful, more majestic and becoming.

Calvin then turns the saying two ways. To the careless it is a warning, since he asks how it comes that wicked men are so much at their ease, and answers that it is because they do not set a high value on the crucified Jesus, so that it is necessary to remind them of a dreadful judgment. To believers it is comfort, that they may now with the eyes of hope look for Christ and patiently wait till he comes. The confession was made in the knowledge that it would be called blasphemy and would bring death, which is what makes it something other than a self-preserving claim.
65:
Lightfoot documents the rule behind the gesture from the Sanhedrin tractate: when witnesses speak out the blasphemy they have heard, all present are bound to rend their clothes, and they do not sew them up again. Ellicott explains its function, that the act was almost as much a formal sign of condemnation as the putting on of the black cap by an English judge. Barnes and Clarke note the legal complication, that strictly it was not lawful for the high priest to rend his clothes (Leviticus 10:6), but Wesley observes that the prohibition concerned his priestly robes, and that rending in cases of blasphemy was thought allowable.

Barnes identifies the assumption on which the whole charge rests and the question it skipped. Christ has, under oath, arrogated to himself what belongs to God; but the only proper point of inquiry was whether he had not given evidence that he was the Messiah, and that therefore his claims were just. That point they never examined, assuming instead that he was an impostor. Robertson states the same circularity: it would not be blasphemy for the real Messiah to make such a claim, but it was intolerable to admit that Jesus could be the Messiah. Clarke quotes Quesnel on the false zeal that serves as a mask of religion, by which men cry heresy, blasphemy and faction in order to oppress the truth.

Calvin presses the hypocrisy of the performance, since the rending plainly shows how boldly and wickedly those who profanely despise God make false pretensions of zeal. It would have been praiseworthy to feel resentment at real blasphemy; but while he refused to make inquiry, Caiaphas contrived an unfounded charge.

Calvin then extracts something useful from the hypocrite. This treacherous man, while assuming a character which did not belong to him, taught the servants of God with what severity of displeasure they ought to regard blasphemies, and so condemns the shameful cowardice of those who are no more affected by an outrage on religion than if they heard buffoons uttering their silly jokes. Real blasphemy would have warranted the torn robe; since the claim was true, the gesture became a witness against the judge rather than the accused.
66:
Gill notes the procedure, that the high priest as president of the court puts the question to the assembly, and they return the verdict. Barnes explains the form of words, that he is found guilty of a crime to which the law annexes death, the law in question being that of blasphemy (Leviticus 24:10–16), which prescribed death by stoning. He then explains why the prescribed penalty was not the one used: the chief priests were unwilling to excite a popular tumult by stoning him, and therefore consulted to deliver him to the Romans to be crucified.

Ellicott glosses the English idiom, since in modern usage guilty is almost always followed by the crime, where older use followed it with the punishment the man deserved (Numbers 35:31). He records that the decision, as far as the meeting went, was unanimous, and sentence was passed; but that carrying it out while the Roman governor was in Jerusalem presented a difficulty, the Jewish rulers ostentatiously disclaiming the power of punishing capital offences (John 18:31). Robertson adds the qualification that makes the unanimity less impressive: they took the vote though it was night and they no longer had the power of death, and it was unanimous save that Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus did not agree, being probably absent and not even invited as men under suspicion.

Clarke marks the collapse of judicial order in a sentence: the judge becomes a party and accuser, and proceeds to the verdict without examining whether all the prophecies concerning the Messiah, and the innumerable miracles he wrought, did not justify him. His conclusion is the principle the trial was designed to avoid, that examination and proof are the ruin of all calumnies.

What the verse records, then, is a sentence passed on a claim nobody tested. The irregularities are cumulative rather than incidental: a night session, an oath that compelled self-incrimination, a claim condemned without inquiry, and the absence of the members likely to object. And the council’s own awareness that it could not execute the sentence already points to the next stage, the delivery of Jesus to Pilate, so that he should die by the Roman death rather than the one their law named.
67:
Chrysostom asks why mockery was added to a death sentence already passed, and answers that it was so we might learn their intemperate spirit: having taken him like a prey, they showed forth their intoxication and gave full swing to their madness. He then praises the men who recorded it, admiring the self-command of the disciples who relate these things disguising nothing and not being ashamed of them, but rather accounting it very great glory that the Lord of the universe should endure to suffer such things for us. His own description keeps the contrast in view, that on the face which the sea had reverenced when it saw it, and from which the sun turned away his rays, they did spit, and struck it with the palms of their hands.

Barnes explains what the gestures meant in that culture, spitting being among the Jews, as among us, significant of the highest contempt and insult (Numbers 12:14; Job 30:10), and buffeting meaning that they struck him with their fists. Clarke parses the two Greek verbs, one meaning to beat with the hand with the fingers clenched and the other to smite the cheek with the open hand. Both of them fasten on the prophecy, where the servant gives his cheek to the smiters and hides not his face from shame and spitting (Isaiah 50:6). Clarke adds what Christ does not do, taking no revenge and bearing all with meekness, without even one word of reply.

Gill supplies the rabbinic measure of the insult, that a man who spits in the presence of his master is guilty of death, so nauseous and filthy was it accounted, and asks how much more it must be to spit in anyone’s face. He connects the result to Isaiah’s word that the servant’s visage was more marred than any man’s (Isaiah 52:14).

Augustine turns the acts into figures of later unbelief, reading the spitting of those who reject the proffered grace and the buffeting of those who prefer their own honour to Christ. The face defiled by their spittle is on this reading the face that bore our shame in order to restore the disfigured image of God in us, which is why the fathers find glory precisely in the indignity rather than in spite of it.
68:
The mockery is aimed at a particular office, and Henry catches the tone of it. They made sport with his prophetical office, having heard him called a prophet and knowing he was famed for wonderful discoveries; this they upbraided him with and pretended to make trial of, as if the divine omniscience must stoop to a piece of children’s play. He compares them to Belshazzar revelling in the temple bowls, and widens the charge to take in all who profanely jest with the scripture and make themselves merry with holy things, which is the same sin in a quieter key. The Gloss says the same more briefly, that it is said in ridicule of his claim to be held as a Prophet by the people.

The taunt depends on the blindfold that Mark and Luke record, which hid the men striking him and so turned the demand into a test with an answer the mockers could check. Barnes explains the gesture that accompanied it, the smiting with the palms of their hands being done as if to prevent a person’s speaking, or to evince abhorrence of what he had spoken; so the blow and the challenge to prophesy worked against each other by design.

What gives the scene its irony is that a prophecy was being fulfilled while they denied his prophetic gift. He had foretold that he would be mocked and spitefully entreated and spitted on (Luke 18:32), and the prediction of Peter’s denial (v.34) was coming true in the courtyard below while they jeered at his sight.

Calvin states what the mockery was meant to establish, that nothing was more unlikely than that he should be a prince of prophets who was not able even to ward off a blow. He then turns the insult inside out: this insolence was turned by the providence of God to a very different purpose, for the face of Christ, dishonoured by spitting and blows, has restored to us that image which had been disfigured, and almost effaced, by sin. The demand to prophesy was a blind man’s jest that announced the truth it derided.
69:
Ellicott harmonises the three denials and places this one. The first came at his entry, in answer to the doorkeeper (John 18:17); the second by the fire, to another girl and the bystanders; the third an hour later in the porch, with the hasty words probably repeated more than once on each occasion. He also probes the motive, judging it was probably shame not less than fear, the same feeling that had once made Peter say that this should be far from his Master (Matthew 16:22); he shrank from the taunts and ridicule which were sure to fall on the followers of one whose career was ending in apparent failure.

Barnes and Robertson note where he was sitting, outside the hall in which the trial proceeded, among the servants at the fire, where the light shone in his face and made him conspicuous to anyone who cared to look.

Henry draws the warnings out of the setting. Bad company leads to sin, and those who needlessly thrust themselves into it may expect to be tempted and ensnared, as Peter was; and it is a great fault to be shy of Christ, since to dissemble our knowledge of him when we are called to own him is in effect to deny him. He also distinguishes this fall from the betrayal, since Peter fell into the sin by surprise and not, as Judas did, by design.

Calvin makes the episode a bright mirror of our weakness and a doctrine which may be applied to the whole Church. He blames the rashness that put Peter there at all: having been warned that he would revolt, he ought rather to have concealed himself, and it frequently happens that believers, under an appearance of virtue, throw themselves within reach of temptation. On the slightness of the assault Calvin is severe, that any man not supported by the hand of God will instantly fall at a slight gale or the rustling of a falling leaf; terrified by a woman’s voice, Peter immediately denies his Master. The disciple who had drawn a sword on an armed cohort (v.51) quailed before an unarmed servant girl, and the watchful prayer he had been told to keep (v.41) was the thing he had not done.
70:
Gill identifies the aggravating circumstance, that the denial was made before them all: as it is to a man’s commendation to profess a good profession of Christ before many witnesses, so it is to his disgrace to deny him before men. He is also careful about what Peter did and did not deny, since he did not deny that Christ was God or the Son of God, but that he was with him, or one of his disciples. Barnes itemises the three forms the denial took across the Gospels, that he denied being a disciple, denied knowing Jesus, and in Mark denied understanding what was meant, and calls all of it palpable falsehood. Robertson treats the words as a familiar manoeuvre, an affectation of extreme ignorance that deceived no one, an easy and ancient dodge.

Clarke numbers the stage in the descent, that before he followed at a distance and now he denies, which is the second gradation in his fall. The sequence the chapter traces is distant following (v.58), denial, denial with an oath (v.72), and denial with cursing (v.74).

Calvin presses the public character of the act, noting that Peter did not even dread a multitude of witnesses, and that the Spirit intended expressly to state this, so that even the presence of men may excite us to hold fast the confession of faith. The harm is not confined to the one denying: if we deny Christ before the weak, they are shaken by our example and give way, and thus we destroy as many souls as we can.

Calvin then weighs the offence exactly. Peter does not deny the whole doctrine of the Gospel, but only that he knew Christ; yet because in the person of Christ he indirectly buries the light of the promised redemption, he is charged with base and shameful treachery. From that Calvin draws a warning against evasion, that the wretched sophists who endeavour to escape by ambiguous expressions gain nothing by their dexterity in fraud, since as soon as we depart from a plain and candid profession of Christ we deprive him of the testimony to which he has a lawful claim.
71:
Gill describes the half-measure Peter took. He did not attempt to go out at the door and run away, choosing rather to keep his ground, but was very uneasy, and so moved into the porch, where he sat pensive. Barnes gives the motive, that Peter was embarrassed and confused by the question, and went from the fire into the porch to prevent his confusion attracting notice, where he expected to be unobserved; and it was in vain. Henry marks the opportunity lost in that movement, since he had gone out into the porch, and had he gone quite off then his second and third denials would have been prevented, but he came in again.

Barnes harmonises the accusers, the charge being repeated by a maid in Matthew and Mark and by a man in Luke, and judges that probably both were done. Robertson notes Peter was not safe out there either, since another maid recognised him and spoke of him with a gesture to those standing about. Mark adds that while he was in the porch the cock crew, which was the first crowing.

Calvin offers a reconstruction that accounts for the variety. It is probable that the statement which proceeded from one maid flew from the lips of one to another, so that the first girl pointed him out to many persons and at several times; and John even has a multitude of men attacking Peter at the second denial, which shows that the word pronounced by the maid was caught up by the men standing by. On Mark’s first cock-crow Calvin explains that Christ’s prediction meant the cock-crowing as a period, which includes many crowings, so that all the Evangelists agree Peter denied him three times before the cock-crowing was over.

The restlessness is the thing the verse records: embarrassed, uneasy, edging away from the fire and yet not leaving the courtyard. It is the posture of a man unwilling either to confess Christ plainly or to quit the place where confession would be demanded of him, and the second accusation found him exactly where the first had left him.
72:
Gill specifies what the oath involved, that he swore by the God of truth and made a solemn appeal to the omniscient God, the searcher of hearts, that he was so far from ever being with Jesus of Nazareth or a disciple of his. Clarke numbers it the third gradation of his iniquity, and explains the mechanism: he has told a lie and now swears to support it, a liar always having some suspicion that his testimony is not credited, and being therefore naturally led to support his assertions by oaths. Ellicott marks how fast the descent now runs, the downward step once taken making the disciple’s fall fatally rapid; forgetful of his Lord’s command forbidding any use of oaths in common speech (Matthew 5:34), he did not shrink from invoking the divine name to attest a falsehood. Robertson notices the phrasing, that Peter refers to Jesus as the man, an expression that could convey contempt.

Calvin states the law of descent he sees at work. A sinner, after having once fallen, is always hurried on from bad to worse, so that those who begin with ordinary offences afterwards rush headlong into the basest crimes, from which at first they would have recoiled with horror. He names the cause as judicial, that this is the just vengeance of God after we have deprived ourselves of the assistance of the Holy Spirit, to allow Satan a violent exercise of power over us.

Calvin applies the rule to this case in particular, since it happens chiefly in a denial of the faith: when a man, through fear of the cross, has turned aside from a pure profession of the gospel, and perceives that his enemies are not yet satisfied, the adversary will proceed farther with him.

Against that Calvin sets a restraining mercy that is easy to overlook. The Lord spared Peter by restraining the tongues of his enemies from making additional attacks upon him, for had more pressed him he would have been ready to deny a hundred or a thousand times; and it is every day necessary for the Lord to bridle Satan, lest he overwhelm us with innumerable temptations. Wesley adds a sober guess about the swearing itself, that Peter may not have been unaccustomed to it before our Lord called him.
73:
What betrays Peter at the third challenge is his accent. Barnes explains that his speech made it manifest he was of the company, since he was a Galilean, and the Galileans were distinguished by some peculiarity of pronunciation, perhaps a rusticity that marked them off from the refinement of the capital. Clarke and Ellicott detail the dialect, that the Galileans had a very corrupt pronunciation, frequently interchanging the gutturals, blending or dividing words so as to render them unintelligible, and changing one sibilant for another. Ellicott adds the aggravating circumstance that the patois was probably stronger when Peter spoke under the influence of strong excitement, so that his denials made his origin plainer than silence would have.

Barnes fixes the interval at about an hour after the previous charge (Luke 22:59), and notes that by this time Peter had returned into the hall and stood warming himself at the fire (John 18:25). John supplies the most dangerous of the accusers, a kinsman of Malchus, the servant whose ear Peter had cut off, who declared he had seen him in the garden (John 18:26). Robertson describes the manner of the challenge, the bystanders coming up and bluntly asserting that he was of a truth one of the followers of Jesus.

Ellicott reads the effect on Peter, that the half-detection the remark implied, and perhaps some sense of shame at the provincialism attracting notice, led to the more vehement denial that followed. Wesley finds providence in the weakness of the case against him: Malchus’s kinsman might have brought a stronger proof than an accent, but such is the overruling providence of God that the world, in the height of its zeal, commonly catches hold of the very weakest of all arguments against the children of God.

The irony is that the disciple who had denied all knowledge of his Master was given away by the speech of his Master’s own country. Flight from the fire had not hidden him and falsehood could not, since the thing that identified him was the one thing he could not leave off doing while he spoke at all.
74:
Gill is careful about the object of the cursing: he cursed himself, making dreadful imprecations and wishes, that all the miseries and calamities he could think of might fall on him if he were one of the disciples of Jesus. Gill insists he did not curse Christ, for in so doing he would have sinned the sin against the Holy Ghost. Robertson describes the state he was in, calling down imprecations on himself in his desperate irritation and loss of self-control at his exposure. Ellicott supposes some common formula of execration, such as God do so to me and more also (1 Kings 19:2). Barnes says he was irritated beyond endurance, and so added to the sin of denying his Lord the deep aggravation of profane cursing and swearing.

Clarke numbers this the fourth and final gradation in the climax of the fall, and draws a sobering inference from the trajectory: from these awful beginnings it is not unfair to conclude that Peter might have gone almost as far as Judas himself, had the traitorous business not already been effected. On the signal, Ellicott notes the Greek has no article, so that a cock crew, and that cock-crowing had become a familiar phrase, as with us, for the earliest hour of dawn.

Calvin marks both the height of the offence and its limit. In this third denial Peter’s unfaithfulness reached its utmost height, since not satisfied with an oath he breaks out into a curse, by which he abandons his body and soul to destruction. And yet the passage shows that when a man, falling through weakness of the flesh, denies the truth though he knows it, this does not amount to blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Matthew 12:31–32); Peter sinned through weakness and not through incurable malice.

Clarke sets the two halves of the verse side by side and finds the wonder in their proportion, that the great Apostle Peter fell through fear of a servant maid and rose through the crowing of a cock. The sign had been named in advance (v.34), so that the means of his recovery was already lodged in the prediction of his fall, and sounded at the moment the fall was complete.
75:
Barnes recounts what Luke adds to the sound of the cock, that Jesus turned and looked upon Peter; and by a tender and compassionate look, a single glance of the eye, the injured Saviour brought to remembrance all Peter’s promises, his own predictions, and the great guilt of the disciple, who then fled from the palace and wept bitterly. Ellicott describes the quality of the glance, full of tenderest pity and deepest sadness, as of one moved not by anger but by sorrow, which recalled him to his better self and opened the flood-gates of penitence.

Barnes draws a series of lessons from the whole episode. There is the danger of self-confidence, since whoever thinks he stands should take heed lest he fall; high privileges do not secure a man from falling; the downward course of sin is easy; true repentance is deep, thorough and bitter; a look from Jesus produces godly sorrow; grief of this kind seeks solitude. He adds the distinction that saves the case from despair, that real Christians may be suffered to go far astray in order to teach them their weakness, Peter’s courage having failed where his faith did not (Luke 22:32). And he closes the door on the obvious abuse, that whoever resolves to sin under the expectation of repenting afterwards cannot be a Christian. He notes too the honesty of the record, Mark’s full account having been written under Peter’s own direction.

Henry hears in the signal a summons rather than a mere reminder, the crowing of a cock serving Peter instead of a John Baptist, as the voice of one calling to repentance; and conscience, he says, should be to us what the cock’s crowing was to him. On the tears he distinguishes their character, that the sorrow was secret and serious, and sets against it the sentence that gives the verse its sting: those who have sinned sweetly must weep bitterly. Henry also records the sequel, that the man who wept so bitterly for denying Christ never denied him again, but confessed him often and openly. Clarke notes the one wise thing Peter did at last, that he went out, leaving the place where he had sinned and the company which had occasioned his transgression.

Ellicott observes what became of the story afterwards, that the record of the fall appears in every Gospel, which indicates that in later years Peter did not shrink from letting men know of his guilt, but sought rather that they might find in him a proof of the mercy and tender pity of his Lord (compare 1 Timothy 1:12–16). Where the traitor’s remorse ended in despair, this penitence ended in restoration.
